Hotels

An operating business that happens to sit in real estate. You re-lease every room every night, so you underwrite operations, brands, and management contracts more than leases.

01Core operating metrics

The hotel equivalents of rent, occupancy and rent growth. You'll hear them in every conversation.

Keys

Number of guest rooms. Deals are priced "per key."

MF analog Units

OccupancyOcc

Rooms sold ÷ rooms available, measured nightly.

MF analog Physical occupancy

Average Daily RateADR

Rooms revenue ÷ rooms sold.

MF analog Average rent per occupied unit

Revenue per Available RoomRevPAR

Occupancy × ADR, or rooms revenue ÷ rooms available. 75% × $200 = $150.

MF analog Effective rent per unit incl. vacancy

Total RevPARTRevPAR

All revenue (rooms, F&B, parking, spa) per available room.

MF analog Total income per unit incl. other income

GOP per Available RoomGOPPAR

Gross operating profit per available room. Owners care about this more than RevPAR.

Flow-through

Share of incremental revenue that becomes incremental profit. Rate-driven growth flows through better than occupancy-driven growth, because every occupied room must be cleaned.

02Benchmarking

Hotels are judged against a comp set of 4–8 competitors using STR (CoStar) data, often called the STAR report. An index of 100 means "fair share."

Comp set

The competing hotels a property is benchmarked against.

Occupancy IndexMPI

Your occupancy ÷ comp set occupancy.

ADR IndexARI

Your ADR ÷ comp set ADR.

RevPAR IndexRGI

Your RevPAR ÷ comp set RevPAR. 115 is a selling point; 85 is a "management or brand upside" story.

Fair share

An index of 100: you capture demand in proportion to your supply.

03The P&L: USALI

The Uniform System of Accounts for the Lodging Industry. It runs top to bottom: departments → undistributed → GOP → fees → fixed charges → EBITDA → reserve → NOI.

Departmental revenue & expense

Rooms, F&B (food & beverage) and other operated departments, each with its own profit line.

Undistributed expenses

Costs no single department owns: A&G (administrative & general), S&M (sales & marketing), POM (property operations & maintenance), utilities.

Gross Operating ProfitGOP

Departmental profit less undistributed expenses. The operator is judged on it.

Fixed charges

Property taxes, insurance, ground rent.

FF&E reserve

Usually ~4% of total revenue, set aside to replace furniture, fixtures and equipment.

NOI (hotel)

Usually after the FF&E reserve. Always confirm which definition an OM uses.

Operating leverage

High fixed costs mean profit swings much more than revenue. A hotel at a 30% margin hurts badly when RevPAR drops.

MF analog MF runs ~55–65% NOI margins

04Product types & chain scales

Full-service

Restaurants, meeting space, banquets. More revenue, much more cost.

Select / focused-service

Limited F&B such as breakfast and a small bar. Think Courtyard or Hilton Garden Inn.

Limited-service

Rooms plus breakfast at most.

Extended-stay

Guests staying 5+ nights, lean staffing (Residence Inn, Homewood Suites).

MF analog Closest hotel product to apartments

Lifestyle / boutique

Design-driven, often soft brands or independents.

Soft brand / collection

A brand affiliation that lets the hotel keep its own name and identity. Popular for conversions.

Chain scale

STR's tiers: Luxury, Upper Upscale, Upscale, Upper Midscale, Midscale, Economy.

05Owner · Brand · Operator

Often three different companies. This is the part multifamily people find least intuitive.

Franchise agreement

Lets the owner use the brand. Owner pays royalty fees (~5–6% of rooms revenue) plus marketing/loyalty fees.

Hotel management agreementHMA

Contract with the company that runs the hotel: the brand itself ("brand-managed") or a third-party manager.

Base management fee

Usually ~2–3% of total revenue.

Incentive management feeIMF

Manager's share of profit above an owner's priority return.

Property Improvement PlanPIP

Renovation the brand requires, usually at sale or franchise renewal. A major acquisition cost line.

Key money

Upfront cash a brand or operator pays the owner to win the contract.

Encumbered vs. unencumbered

Whether the hotel is sold subject to an existing management agreement. Unencumbered trades at a premium.

Area of protection

Radius in which the franchisor won't license the same brand to a competitor.

06Revenue management & demand

Transient

Individual travelers: BAR (Best Available Rate), corporate negotiated, OTA (Expedia, Booking.com), GDS (travel-agent systems).

Group

Blocks of 10+ rooms for conferences or weddings.

SMERF

Social, military, educational, religious, fraternal groups. Price-sensitive business that fills soft nights.

On-the-books & paceOTB

Bookings for future dates vs. the same point last year.

Pickup

New bookings over a period.

Attrition

A group books fewer rooms than it contracted for.

Displacement

Whether a low-rate group pushes out higher-paying transient guests.

Compression night

A sold-out citywide event where you can push rate hard.

Shoulder season

Between peak and off-peak.

Walk a guest

You overbooked and must relocate a guest to another hotel.

07Valuation & credit

Price per key

The headline valuation unit, compared against replacement cost per key.

Cap rate on T-12

Applied to trailing-twelve-month NOI after reserve. Hotel caps run above multifamily for volatility.

Ramp-up / stabilization

Period after an opening, renovation or rebrand before the hotel reaches its run-rate.

Debt yield

NOI ÷ loan. Lenders want it meaningfully higher on hotels than apartments, often low double digits or more.

Franchisor comfort letter

Keeps the brand affiliation in place if the lender forecloses.

Cash management trigger

Moves the loan into a lockbox or cash sweep if DSCR or debt yield drops below a threshold.

Seasonality

Big monthly cash-flow swings, so reserves and covenant testing periods matter.

Pre-opening expense

Hiring, training and sales launch before the first guest arrives.

No hotel terms match that filter.

Case 1 · Ground-up development

150-key upscale select-service

IC memo · live model

A developer controls a 3-acre pad near a growing hospital campus and corporate office park in a secondary market. No new hotel supply in 8 years; the comp set runs 72% occupancy at a $185 ADR. Plan: a 5-story, wood-frame, upscale select-service hotel at the Hilton Garden Inn / Courtyard tier.

Step 1Feasibility before any spreadsheet

  • Demand generators. Hospital visitors and traveling nurses, corporate transient from the office park, weekend youth sports and weddings. Weekday corporate plus weekend leisure is the ideal mix.
  • Supply pipeline. What's approved or under construction within 5–10 miles?
  • Brand selection. Which flag has the strongest loyalty contribution here, and is the area of protection open?
  • Penetration. New hotels open below fair share and ramp above it: MPI ~85 in Year 1 rising to ~105 at stabilization.

  • Rate beats occupancy. Higher ADR flows through at ~80% because the extra revenue carries few new costs. Extra occupancy flows through at only ~55–60%: every occupied room has to be cleaned, staffed and paid a franchise fee.
  • Ways to fix it: a PILOT or tax abatement, key money from the brand, a dual-brand building, C-PACE financing, land contributed as equity, or a cheaper brand prototype.

Case 2 · Distressed acquisition & value-add

220-key full-service REO

IC memo · live model

A 1989-vintage full-service hotel with 12,000 SF of meeting space and a restaurant. The prior owner couldn't fund a required PIP, so the brand terminated the franchise. Revenue collapsed, the CMBS loan defaulted, and the special servicer foreclosed. We're bidding on the REO asset.

Step 1Why did it fail?

  • Capital failure (undercapitalized owner): fixable. This is our thesis.
  • Operator failure: fixable by replacing management.
  • Market failure (demand left for good): not fixable by us. Walk away.

The comp set is healthy at ~$112 RevPAR, which points to an asset-specific problem.

Step 2T-12 in-place performance

Trailing 12 monthsValue
Pricing a negative-NOI hotelYou can't apply a cap rate. Buyers price on price per key against replacement cost (a comparable new full-service hotel might cost $350k+/key) and on stabilized yield on total cost.

Step 3Business plan & all-in basis

  1. Re-flag with an upscale conversion or collection brand; negotiate the PIP and ask for key money.
  2. Replace the manager with a third-party operator with a strong record for the new brand.
  3. Right-size F&B: swap the three-meal restaurant for a lobby bar and grab-and-go; invest in banquets and meetings, where the margin is.
  4. Fix deferred maintenance from the PCA: roof, elevators, PTACs/HVAC.
  5. Renovate in phases, floor by floor. Rooms out of order (OOO) reduce available room nights, so model them.
Line item$MPer key

T-12Yr 1 (reno)Yr 2Yr 3 stabilized

Step 6Downside: what IC will challenge

What moves the dealNOIYield on basisLevered IRRMultiple

Distressed-specific diligence

  • Liquor license transfer often isn't automatic; you may need an interim concession agreement to keep the bar open.
  • Old HMA: confirm it was terminated in foreclosure and doesn't bind you.
  • Union / CBA and WARN Act: are you assuming a collective bargaining agreement? Layoffs can trigger notice rules.
  • Advance deposits and group business on the books: know the liability for weddings and conferences already booked.
  • Guest reviews: a 2.5 rating takes time to recover even after renovation.
  • Brand approval of you, the PIP and the operator before closing, or you're buying an independent.
Credit lensAn investor could instead buy the defaulted note from the special servicer at a discount (loan-to-own) and take title by foreclosure or deed-in-lieu, often with a court-appointed receiver running the hotel in the interim.

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer.

Q1Hotel A runs 85% occupancy at a $180 ADR. Hotel B runs 70% at $230. Which has the higher RevPAR, and which would you rather own?

Show answer

A: $153.00 RevPAR. B: $161.00. B wins on RevPAR, and it gets there with fewer occupied rooms, so it cleans fewer rooms and its flow-through to profit is likely better. But check why B's occupancy is low: if it's a demand or reputation problem, A may be the more durable asset. Compare GOPPAR, not just RevPAR.

Q2A seller advertises an RGI of 82. Red flag or opportunity?

Show answer

Both, until you know why. Check whether the comp set is fair (a seller can pick an aggressive one), whether the gap is in MPI or ARI, the condition of the rooms, the brand's loyalty contribution, the operator's track record, and guest reviews. If the gap comes from fixable management or capital issues, it's upside. If it comes from location or a weak flag you can't change, it's a value trap.

Q3Why would a buyer pay more for an unencumbered hotel?

Show answer

Without an existing management agreement, the buyer can pick its own operator (or self-manage), negotiate fees, and rebrand freely. An encumbered hotel locks the buyer into a manager and fee structure that may be long-term and expensive to terminate, which limits the value-add plan and future exit options.

Q4In Case 1, why does +$10 of ADR create more value than +4 points of occupancy with similar revenue?

Show answer

A higher rate adds revenue with almost no added cost; only variable fees (franchise, management) scale with it, so ~80% flows to NOI. Extra occupancy brings housekeeping, laundry, amenities and other per-room costs, so only ~55–60% flows through.

01Measuring space

Rentable SFRSF

The space a tenant pays for, including its share of common areas.

MF analog Unit count / net rentable SF

Usable SFUSF

The space a tenant actually occupies.

Load factor / loss factor

Share of lobbies, corridors and mechanical rooms added on top of USF. A 15% load bills 10,000 USF as ~11,500 RSF.

BOMA

The industry standard for measuring office space.

Floorplate

Size and shape of one floor. Large, efficient floorplates with good column spacing attract big tenants.

Core-to-glass depth

Distance from the building core to the windows. Drives natural light, office appeal and residential conversion feasibility.

02Building quality & market

Class A / B / C

A relative grade of location, age, systems and amenities within a market.

Trophy

The very top of Class A: newest, best-located, highest rents.

Flight to quality

Tenants shrink their footprint while moving into newer, better buildings. Since the pandemic, the best buildings do well and older commodity buildings struggle.

Sublease space

Space tenants are trying to offload, usually at a discount, competing with your direct space.

Shadow vacancy

Space that's leased but unused. It shows up as sublease supply or non-renewals later.

Utilization

How much of its space a tenant actually uses (often from badge-swipe data). A tenant at 30% is a likely non-renewal.

Amenities

Fitness, tenant lounge, conference center, roof terrace. Now an expectation for Class A.

03Lease structures

Full Service GrossFSG

Landlord pays operating expenses and taxes out of the rent.

Triple netNNN

Tenant pays its share of opex and taxes on top of base rent.

Modified gross

Somewhere in between: some expenses passed through, some not.

Base year / expense stop

Tenant pays only increases in opex above the first-year level (or a fixed stop).

Escalations

Annual rent bumps, e.g. 3% per year, or pass-through of expense increases.

Expense recoveries

What landlords collect back from tenants for opex and taxes.

Termination / contraction option

Tenant's right to leave early or give back space, usually for a fee. Lenders discount leases that have them.

ROFO / ROFR

Right of first offer / first refusal on adjacent or expansion space.

04Leasing costs

The costs that separate office from multifamily. A 10-year lease can cost the landlord a year or more of rent before the tenant moves in.

Tenant improvement allowanceTI

Landlord's contribution to building out the tenant's space, quoted in $/RSF.

MF analog Unit turn cost, but 10–50x larger

Leasing commissionLC

Paid to tenant and landlord brokers, usually up front, as a % of total lease value or $/RSF per year.

Free rent / abatement

Months of no rent at the start of a lease.

MF analog Concessions ("one month free")

Face (headline) rent

The quoted rent.

Net effective rentNER

Face rent after deducting free rent, TI and LC, spread over the term. Sophisticated landlords track NER.

Spec suites

Pre-built, move-in-ready small suites. Key tool for leasing up a value-add building.

Work letter

Lease exhibit defining who builds out the space and what the TI covers.

Cold / warm shell, turnkey

Delivery condition: raw space, basic systems in place, or fully finished by the landlord.

05Rent roll & underwriting

Weighted avg. lease termWALT

Remaining lease term, weighted by rent or SF. Long WALT = durable income.

Rollover

Leases expiring in a given period. A big rollover year is a risk event.

Downtime

Months of vacancy between a tenant leaving and a new one paying rent.

Renewal probability

Share of expiring tenants expected to stay. Renewals cost far less TI and LC.

Market leasing assumptionsMLA

The model's set of rent, term, TI, LC, free rent, downtime and renewal assumptions for each space.

Blend-and-extend

Lower a tenant's rent now in exchange for a longer term.

TI/LC reserve

Below-NOI reserve ($/RSF per year) for future leasing costs. Office is capital-intensive even when stabilized.

Dark value

What the building is worth empty. A floor on value for a distressed asset.

06Development & lender paperwork

Spec (speculative)

Built without tenants signed. Rarely financeable for office today.

Pre-leased

A portion leased before construction starts. Lenders often require 40–50%+.

Build-to-suit

Built for one specific tenant.

Anchor tenant

The large, creditworthy tenant that makes the project financeable.

Merchant build

Develop, lease up and sell at stabilization to a core buyer.

Estoppel

Tenant certifies its lease terms are as represented.

SNDA

Subordination, non-disturbance and attornment agreement between tenant and lender.

Carry / completion / repayment guarantees

Sponsor recourse that's standard on office construction loans.

07Distress & credit

Special servicer

Manages defaulted CMBS loans: modifies, forecloses or sells them.

REO

Real estate owned: property a lender took back through foreclosure.

Loan-to-own

Buy the defaulted note at a discount, then take title.

Discounted payoffDPO

Lender accepts less than the full balance to retire the loan.

Extend and pretend

A loan modification that pushes out maturity hoping values recover.

Appraisal reduction

A new, lower appraisal on a troubled CMBS loan that shifts losses down the capital stack.

Leasing hurdles / cash sweep

Value-add loan terms: future funding tied to leasing milestones; excess cash trapped if leasing lags.

No office terms match that filter.

Case 1 · Ground-up development

250,000 RSF Class A, 44% pre-leased

IC memo · live model

A 12-story Class A building with structured parking in a growing urban submarket. A law firm anchor has signed for 110,000 RSF (44%) on a 15-year lease; the remaining 140,000 RSF is spec. Newer Class A buildings in the submarket are well leased while older buildings sit at high vacancy.

Run the case with your numbers

Change any assumption and every table, return and the deal sheet below recalculate. Monthly model: equity funds first, then the construction loan; the building sells at the month you set.

More assumptions

Fixed in the model: 5% hard-cost contingency, 1% loan fee, 6-month anchor build-out, 3-month spec build-out, rents flat during the hold. LC is paid on the first 10 years of rent (3% bumps). Spec TI and LC are spent only on space that leases; landlord pays opex on the whole building from completion (full service gross). Free rent still owed at sale is credited to the buyer.

Step 1The anchor matters more than anything

Construction lenders rarely finance spec office today. Many require meaningful pre-leasing, often 40–50%+, from a creditworthy tenant. The anchor lease effectively is the collateral, so underwriting starts there:

  • What is the tenant's credit quality?
  • Does the lease have termination or contraction options, or a ROFO/ROFR on expansion space?
  • What is the anchor's TI package, and when does rent start?

Office-only weightTI and LC are ~22% of the budget. In multifamily, leasing costs are a rounding error.

Case 2 · Distressed acquisition & reposition

300,000 RSF Class B → A–

IC memo · live model

A 1980s-vintage 300,000 RSF Class B tower in a solid submarket near transit. 45% leased with a short WALT; the largest tenant (40,000 RSF) has given notice to vacate in 12 months. The CMBS loan defaulted and the special servicer is selling it as REO. Class A in the submarket leases at $60+ FSG; Class B struggles at ~$40.

Step 1The thesis test

  • Is the location good enough to compete for Class A tenants? A reposition can't fix a bad location.
  • Can the building physically become A–? Ceiling heights, column spacing, floorplate size, window line.
  • What's the alternative use? If the office plan fails, could it convert to residential? Floorplate depth, window line and plumbing decide that, and a credible conversion option sets a floor on value.

Step 2In-place financials

$M

Step 3The repositioning plan

  • Base building: new lobby and storefront, facade refresh, elevator modernization, HVAC and air-quality upgrades, new restrooms.
  • Amenity floor: fitness, tenant lounge, conference center, roof terrace.
  • Spec suites: ~40,000 RSF of move-in-ready small suites.
  • Rebrand with a new building name and a top leasing agent.
  • Renew the right tenants early with blend-and-extend deals.

Office-specific diligence

  • Lease abstracts and estoppels: confirm rent, options, and any termination or contraction rights.
  • Rollover schedule: who leaves, when, and their utilization.
  • Base year resets: new leases reset base years and reduce recovery income.
  • Tax appeal: a distressed price often supports a lower assessment, which goes straight to NOI.
  • Building systems and emissions laws: in NYC, Local Law 97 fines can be a real cost for older buildings.
  • Floorplate efficiency: drives both office appeal and conversion potential.
Credit lensBuyers can enter through the debt instead of the deed: buy the defaulted note (loan-to-own), negotiate a discounted payoff, or work a loan modification with the special servicer. Office has been the main source of CMBS distress this cycle, so expect this vocabulary in credit interviews.

Deal sheet

Stabilized

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer.

Q1Two offers on the same space: Tenant A at $70 face with 14 months free and $120 TI; Tenant B at $64 face with 6 months free and $80 TI. Both 10 years, 3% bumps, 5% LC. Which is better?

Show answer

Run both through the NER calculator. A: ~$56/yr effective. B: ~$58.50/yr. B wins despite the $6 lower face rent, and it also puts less capital at risk up front ($148 vs. $242/RSF of free rent, TI and LC) and leaves a face rent that's easier to renew. Face rent alone would have picked A.

Q2A broker markets a Class B building at a 7% cap on in-place NOI. What do you check before believing it?

Show answer

The rollover schedule and WALT (who leaves in the next 24 months), tenant utilization and any termination options, whether in-place rents are above market, the TI/LC needed to re-lease, deferred capex, and sublease competition. Rebuild forward NOI after known move-outs, then compare price per RSF to replacement cost and dark value.

Q3Why does office development produce weak IRRs even when the spread clears 150 bps?

Show answer

Duration. Construction plus lease-up plus free rent burn-off can take ~5 years before stabilization, and equity is usually funded first. The same profit spread over more years produces a lower IRR, and every month of slower leasing adds carry.

Q4From a lender's view, what's the biggest difference between Case 1 and Case 2 risk?

Show answer

Case 1 has completion and lease-up risk on new product, mitigated by the anchor lease and sponsor guarantees. Case 2 has execution and leasing risk on old product with negative forward NOI, so the lender relies on basis, future-funding hurdles and cash sweeps. In both, the loan only refinances if the space gets leased at an acceptable net effective rent.

01Product types

"Industrial" covers very different buildings. The type tells you who the tenants are and what they will pay for.

Bulk distribution / big box

Large warehouses, usually 250,000–1,000,000+ SF, near interstates. Tenants are retailers, e-commerce and 3PLs moving goods regionally.

Last-mile / infill

Smaller, often older buildings inside dense metros, close to consumers. Location matters more than specs, and land is scarce.

MF analog Infill urban vs. suburban garden

Small-bay / shallow-bay

Multi-tenant buildings with suites of roughly 5,000–50,000 SF. Many small tenants, more management, strong rent growth.

Flex / light industrial

Mix of office and warehouse space, usually more finished office, lower clear heights. Tenants: R&D, showrooms, light assembly.

Manufacturing

Purpose-built for production: heavy power, cranes, special floors. Often single-tenant, harder to re-lease.

Cold storage

Refrigerated and freezer warehouses for food and pharma. Costs 2–3x a dry warehouse to build; fewer tenants, higher rents.

Industrial outdoor storageIOS

Mostly paved, fenced land with a small building, used to park trucks, trailers and equipment. Priced per acre, low building coverage.

Cross-dock / truck terminal

Long, narrow buildings with doors on both sides so freight moves straight from inbound to outbound trucks.

Multi-story warehouse

Ramped buildings with truck access to upper floors. Built only where land is very expensive.

02Building specs

Tenants shop industrial by spec sheet. A missing spec can rule a building out entirely.

Clear height

Usable height from floor to the lowest overhead obstruction (joists, sprinklers). Modern bulk is 36–40'; older buildings are often 18–24'. More height means more pallets stacked per SF.

MF analog Ceiling height, but it changes what the space can be used for

Dock-high doors

Loading doors at truck-bed height (~4'), so trailers load straight onto the warehouse floor.

Drive-in / grade-level doors

Ground-level doors that trucks or forklifts drive through.

Dock ratio

Dock doors per SF of building, e.g. 1 per 5,000 SF for e-commerce or 1 per 10,000 SF for storage.

Truck court

Paved area in front of the docks where trucks maneuver. 130' is the minimum; 185' allows a row of trailer parking.

Trailer parking / stalls

Space to park trailers that aren't docked. A major differentiator for logistics tenants.

Column spacing / speed bay

Distance between columns, e.g. 56' × 50', with a wider 60' "speed bay" along the docks for staging freight.

ESFR sprinklers

Early Suppression, Fast Response sprinklers. Allow high-piled storage without in-rack sprinklers. Standard in modern warehouses.

Slab thickness

Floor thickness, e.g. 7–8" reinforced concrete. Matters for heavy racking and automation.

Building depth / loading config

Rear-load (docks on one side), cross-dock (both sides), or front-load. Deeper buildings suit bulk; shallower suit small-bay.

Office finish %

Share of the building that's finished office, typically 2–10%. Kept low because warehouse tenants don't pay much for office.

Power

Electrical service in amps and voltage (e.g. 2,000A, 480V 3-phase). Automation, EV truck charging and cold storage need much more.

Site coverage ratio

Building footprint ÷ land area. ~40–50% for modern distribution; IOS is often under 10%.

Tilt-up construction

Concrete wall panels cast on site and lifted into place. Fast and cheap, the standard way to build warehouses.

03Leasing

Triple netNNN

Tenant pays base rent plus its share of taxes, insurance and common area maintenance. The landlord's NOI is close to base rent.

MF analog The opposite of an apartment, where the landlord pays opex

Rent quoting

Usually $/SF per year NNN (e.g. "$9.50 net"). Some West Coast markets quote monthly (e.g. "$1.25/SF/month").

Annual escalations

Fixed bumps, often 3–5% per year in recent leases.

Mark-to-market

Gap between in-place rent and today's market rent. "40% mark-to-market" means leases roll up 40% when they expire. The core industrial value-add thesis.

CAM / recoveries

Common area maintenance and other costs billed back to tenants. On vacant space the landlord eats them.

Spec vs. build-to-suitBTS

Spec: built with no tenant signed. BTS: designed and built for one tenant, often with a long lease.

Third-party logistics3PL

Companies that run warehouses for other businesses. A large share of industrial demand; their credit varies.

Single-tenant risk

A one-tenant building is 100% leased or 0% leased. Credit quality, lease term and renewal odds dominate the underwriting.

Divisibility

Whether a big building can be split for 2–4 tenants: multiple office corners, separate dock areas and power. Widens the tenant pool.

Absorption & deliveries

Absorption: net change in occupied SF. Deliveries: new SF completed. Deliveries above absorption push vacancy up.

04Land & development

Land price per acre

How industrial land trades. Infill land can be worth more than the building on it.

Entitlements

Zoning and approvals to build. Many towns now resist new warehouses, which makes entitled land valuable.

Horizontal / site work

Grading, utilities, roads, stormwater and paving before the building goes up. A big share of industrial cost.

Shell cost

Cost of the building envelope: slab, walls, roof, sprinklers, docks. Office and TI are separate.

Yield on cost & spread

Stabilized NOI ÷ total cost, compared with the exit cap. Industrial developers typically want 100–150+ bps.

Covered land play

Buying an older building mainly for the land underneath, collecting rent until redevelopment makes sense.

Functional obsolescence

A building that still stands but doesn't meet modern needs: low clear height, shallow truck court, few docks.

Phase I / Phase II ESA

Environmental site assessments. Older industrial sites often carry contamination risk (underground tanks, solvents, PFAS).

05Data centers (special topic)

Data centers sit in the industrial world but are priced on power, not floor area. Full case on the Data center tab.

Critical IT loadMW

Power available to run the servers, in megawatts. The unit everything is priced in: "a 60 MW campus."

Power usage effectivenessPUE

Total facility power ÷ IT power. 1.2–1.5 is typical; the extra is cooling and losses.

Hyperscale

Huge campuses leased to cloud and AI giants (often 10–15-year leases, investment-grade credit).

Colocation (colo)

Multi-tenant facilities. Retail colo leases racks or cages to many customers; wholesale colo leases whole halls.

Powered shell vs. turnkey

Powered shell: building plus utility power, tenant installs the electrical and cooling gear. Turnkey: landlord delivers it all.

$/kW/month

How rent is quoted: dollars per kilowatt of IT capacity per month.

Redundancy (N, N+1, 2N)

Backup level for power and cooling. N+1 has one spare unit; 2N duplicates the whole system.

Rack density

Power per server rack. Traditional racks use 5–15 kW; AI racks can exceed 100 kW and need liquid cooling.

Time to power

How soon the utility can deliver the needed megawatts. Today's biggest constraint; sites with power secured command a premium.

White space / gray space

White space holds servers. Gray space holds electrical and mechanical equipment.

06Valuation & credit

Price per SF vs. replacement cost

Buyers compare price to what it would cost to build new today, including land.

Going-in cap vs. mark-to-market

Infill buildings often trade at low going-in caps because buyers pay for future rent growth.

Dark value

Value with the building empty. Critical for single-tenant underwriting.

Credit tenant lease

A long lease to an investment-grade tenant. Lenders may underwrite the tenant more than the building.

Debt yield (industrial)

Industrial is seen as the most financeable commercial asset; lenders accept lower debt yields than for hotels or office.

Structural reserve

Non-recoverable reserve for roof, structure and parking, often $0.10–0.20/SF per year.

No industrial terms match that filter.

Submarket vacancy has come back down after the 2023–24 supply wave, and few large buildings are under construction. Plan: a 400,000 SF cross-dock warehouse built on spec.

Case 2 · Value-add acquisition

220,000 SF 1980s infill warehouse

IC memo · live model

A 1980s-vintage, 220,000 SF multi-tenant warehouse on 10 acres, 15 minutes from a dense metro core. It's 85% leased to five tenants at an average $8.50 NNN, on leases signed years ago. Renovated buildings nearby lease at $14.50. The owner deferred capital for a decade. Specs are dated: 24' clear, 110' truck courts, older sprinklers.

Step 1Why buy an obsolete box?

  • Location can't be rebuilt. Zoning and land costs make new infill warehouses nearly impossible to build here. Last-mile tenants need to be close to customers more than they need 36' clear.
  • Rents are far below market. In-place $8.50 vs. market $14.50 is a ~71% mark-to-market. Every lease that rolls is a large NOI increase.
  • The building is the right size for small and mid-size tenants, which is the deepest part of infill demand.
  • Downside floor: if the building disappoints, the land itself (as IOS or a future redevelopment site) still has value.

Step 2In-place financials

$M

Step 3Business plan

  1. Roof replacement and building envelope repairs. A 30-year-old roof is the first thing a tenant's inspector will flag.
  2. Sprinkler upgrade toward ESFR where the structure allows, so tenants can store higher-hazard goods.
  3. LED lighting, skylights, paint and new storefronts to make it look like a renovated building.
  4. Loading: new dock levelers and seals, plus 8 added dock doors.
  5. Yard: repave the truck courts and convert unused land to trailer parking.
  6. Re-lease each suite to market as leases roll, with 5-year terms and 4% bumps.

Line item$MPer SF

Replacement cost is roughly $275+/SF (infill land at ~$3M/acre plus a new building), and the zoning likely wouldn't allow a new one anyway.

  • Rent comps for comparable specs: renovated 1980s buildings, not new 36' product.
  • Tenant-by-tenant rollover: who renews, who leaves, and how long each suite sits empty.
  • Environmental: Phase I, and likely Phase II on an older industrial site (tanks, solvents, PFAS).
  • Zoning: is the use legal non-conforming? Could it be rebuilt after a casualty?
  • Physical: roof, slab condition, sprinkler capacity, power and the stormwater system.
  • Alternative use: IOS or redevelopment value of the land as a floor.

Special topic · Data center development

60 MW hyperscale campus, Phase 1

IC memo · illustrative

Megawatts to rent

Data centers are leased by power, not floor area. Convert critical IT megawatts into annual rent and the total power the utility must deliver.

Annual rent
–
Utility power
–
Rent yield on cost
–
Read
–

A developer controls 150 acres outside a major data center market, with a signed agreement for 200 MW of utility power delivered in phases. Phase 1 is a 60 MW critical IT building, fully pre-leased before construction to an investment-grade cloud provider on a 15-year NNN lease, delivered turnkey.

Step 1Why data centers are different

  • Power is the scarce input, not land or buildings. Utilities in top markets now quote years for new capacity. A site with power secured is worth far more than one without.
  • Cost and value are per MW. A 60 MW building might be 400,000–600,000 SF, but nobody prices it per SF.
  • Most of the cost is equipment: switchgear, transformers, generators, UPS systems and cooling. The building shell is a small share.
  • Tenants are few and huge. Hyperscalers pre-lease whole buildings, so the deal is a credit underwriting as much as a real estate one.
  • AI changed the specs. Training and inference clusters run much denser racks, which pushes toward liquid cooling and more power per building.

Step 2Development budget

Line item$MPer MW
Land (Phase 1 share)30$0.5M
Substation & utility interconnection60$1.0M
Building shell & site work90$1.5M
Electrical & mechanical (switchgear, UPS, generators, cooling)480$8.0M
Soft costs, fees & developer fee50$0.8M
Contingency40$0.7M
Financing fees & capitalized interest50$0.8M
Total800~$13.3M
Where the money goesAbout 60% of cost is electrical and mechanical equipment, and the shell is about 11%. Long lead times on transformers and switchgear (often 1–3 years) mean equipment is ordered before the building is designed in detail.

Step 3Lease and NOI

$M / yrNote
Base rent: 60,000 kW × $115/kW/month × 1282.815-year NNN, ~3% bumps
Power & operating costs–Tenant pays the power bill and reimburses opex
Non-recoverable costs & reserve(3.8)~5% of rent
Stabilized NOI79.0

Rent typically starts as each data hall is delivered, so a phased building ramps over several months rather than flipping on at once.

Step 4Spread & returns

Yield on cost = 79.0 ÷ 800 = ~9.9%. A stabilized building on a long investment-grade lease might trade at ~6.25%, a ~365 bps spread. Stabilized value is ~$1.26B, roughly $460M above cost.

Capital stack: a construction loan at 65% LTC ($520M) and $280M of equity. Lenders lend this much because the lease is signed with a strong tenant before construction. At stabilization the owner sells, recapitalizes with a partner, or refinances (data center ABS and CMBS are now active markets).

Yield on cost
~9.9%vs. ~6.25% exit cap
Equity multiple
~2.5xif delivered on time
Levered IRR
35%+~3 years to stabilization

These spreads are why so much capital wants into the sector. They also tell you the risks are real; otherwise the returns would be competed away.

Step 5What can go wrong

RiskWhat it looks like
Power delayUtility or substation slips a year; the building is finished but can't run
Delivery penaltiesHyperscale leases often carry late-delivery credits or termination rights
Equipment supplyTransformer or generator lead times stretch; costs rise
Tenant concentrationOne tenant is 100% of income; its strategy shifts
Technical obsolescenceCooling and density needs change faster than a 15-year lease
PermittingZoning, site plan, building, environmental and air permits (for diesel backup generators) take longer than planned; a denial or new local moratorium can stop the project
Local oppositionConcerns about noise, water use and grid strain slow approvals
Residual valueWhat the building is worth if the tenant leaves after year 15
Credit lensThe lender underwrites the tenant's credit and the lease terms first, then completion risk. Key questions: Is power contractually secured on a schedule that matches delivery? What happens to rent if delivery is late? Is there a completion guarantee? And how much of the loan is repaid by the time the lease expires, since that's when residual value risk shows up.

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer.

Q1Why does a 36' clear warehouse rent for more than a 24' one of the same footprint?

Show answer

Tenants pay for cubic storage, not floor area. Going from 24' to 36' adds roughly 2–3 levels of pallet racking, so the same floor holds far more goods and the tenant's cost per pallet falls. Modern buildings usually come with better docks, truck courts and sprinklers too.

Q2An infill warehouse is offered at a 4.0% cap when debt costs 7%. Why would anyone buy it?

Show answer

Because in-place rents are far below market and the leases are short. The buyer is pricing the NOI after rents roll up (mark-to-market), plus the scarcity of infill land. The risk is that market rent falls or the leases don't roll on schedule, leaving negative leverage for longer.

Q3A single-tenant warehouse is 100% leased with 2 years left. What do you need to know before lending on it?

Show answer

Tenant credit, its likelihood of renewing (how much it has invested in the space, its operations there), the market rent versus its rent, the building's specs against current demand, and the dark value if it leaves. A lender will often size to dark value or require reserves or a cash sweep ahead of expiration.

Q4A 60 MW data hall rents at $115/kW/month. What is annual rent, and what is the utility delivering at a 1.3 PUE?

Show answer

60,000 kW × $115 × 12 = $82.8M a year. Total facility power is 60 × 1.3 = 78 MW, because cooling and losses add 30% on top of the IT load. Try it in the calculator on the Data center tab.

Q5Why do data center construction lenders lend 65%+ of cost when spec office lenders struggle at 50%?

Show answer

The data center is fully pre-leased to an investment-grade tenant on a long NNN lease before construction, so the income is contractual. Spec office has no signed income for most of the space. The data center lender's main risks are completion and power timing, not leasing.

Retail · Week 4

Retail

A merchandising business. The anchor brings the traffic, the small shops pay the rent, and the lease clauses that tie them together decide what happens when one tenant leaves.

Tenant health & percentage rent

Is the rent sustainable for the tenant, and does it owe percentage rent? Occupancy cost = (base rent + CAM, taxes, insurance) ÷ sales. Natural breakpoint = base rent ÷ percentage rate.

01Center formats

Retail is classified by size and anchor type. The format tells you who shops there and why.

Neighborhood center

30,000–150,000 SF, usually anchored by a grocery store. Daily-needs shopping within a few miles. The best-performing format today.

Community center

125,000–400,000 SF with several anchors such as a grocer, discount department store, off-price apparel and home goods.

Power center

250,000–600,000+ SF dominated by big-box category killers (electronics, home improvement, sporting goods) with little small-shop space.

Regional / super-regional mall

Enclosed centers of 400,000–1,000,000+ SF anchored by department stores. Graded A to D; the A malls still thrive, many lower-grade malls are being redeveloped.

Lifestyle center

Open-air, upscale, restaurant- and experience-heavy. Often part of mixed-use projects.

Unanchored strip

Small row of shops with no anchor, relying on visibility and convenience. Higher turnover, local tenants.

Single-tenant net leaseSTNL

One tenant (pharmacy, QSR, dollar store, bank) on a long NNN or absolute net lease. Bought largely on tenant credit.

MF analog None: closer to a bond than a building

Outparcel / pad site

A separate lot at the front of a center for a drive-thru, bank or restaurant. Sold or ground-leased.

02Tenants & merchandising

Anchor

The large tenant that draws traffic (grocer, Target, Home Depot). Pays low rent per SF because it creates the traffic everyone else needs.

Junior anchor

Mid-size box of roughly 10,000–40,000 SF: off-price apparel, pet, fitness, discount stores.

Shop space / in-line

Small units (1,000–5,000 SF) between anchors. Highest rent per SF and the main source of NOI.

Shadow anchor

A big store next to your center that you don't own but whose traffic you benefit from.

Tenant mix / merchandising

Choosing which uses go where so they feed each other's traffic. Landlords curate it like a store curates products.

Necessity / daily-needs retail

Grocery, pharmacy, services, restaurants, medical. Hard to replace with e-commerce.

Medical retail (medtail)

Urgent care, dental, physical therapy and similar uses in retail space. Sticky tenants with high build-out.

QSR

Quick-service restaurant. Drive-thru QSRs are the most sought-after pad tenants.

National / regional / local tenant

Credit and stickiness generally fall from national chains to local "mom-and-pop" tenants. Locals often pay more rent per SF.

03Lease clauses

Retail leases are full of clauses that link tenants together. Reading them is most of retail diligence.

CAM

Common area maintenance: parking lot, landscaping, lighting, security, snow removal. Billed back to tenants by pro-rata share.

Pro-rata share

Tenant SF ÷ center GLA (or a defined denominator). Determines its share of CAM, taxes and insurance.

CAM admin fee & caps

Landlords often add a 10–15% admin fee to CAM. Anchors often negotiate fixed or capped CAM, which leaves the landlord paying the rest.

CAM reconciliation

Year-end true-up of estimated vs. actual expenses. Errors here are a common source of tenant disputes and audits.

Percentage rent

Extra rent equal to a % of sales above a breakpoint. Natural breakpoint = base rent ÷ % rate.

Sales reporting

Lease requirement for tenants to report sales, used for percentage rent and to monitor tenant health.

Occupancy cost ratio

Total occupancy cost (rent + CAM + tax + insurance) ÷ sales. Above ~12–15% for most shop tenants is a warning sign.

Co-tenancy clause

Lets a tenant pay reduced rent or leave if a named anchor closes or occupancy falls below a threshold. Turns one vacancy into many rent cuts.

Go-dark / continuous operation

Whether a tenant may close its store while still paying rent. A dark anchor that pays rent still kills traffic.

Exclusive use clause

Prevents the landlord from leasing to a competitor (e.g. only one grocer, one pharmacy, one coffee shop).

Radius restriction

Stops a tenant from opening another store within a set distance, protecting the center's sales.

Kick-out clause

Lets a tenant terminate if sales stay below a set level.

REA / OEA

Reciprocal (or operating) easement agreement among owners in a center, governing parking, access, signage and permitted uses. Anchors often hold approval rights over changes.

Vanilla / white box

Delivery condition: finished walls, HVAC, restroom and basic lighting, ready for the tenant's fit-out.

04Site & trade area

Gross leasable areaGLA

Total floor area tenants can lease. Retail's SF unit.

Trade area

Where the center's shoppers come from, often a 3- or 5-mile radius or a drive-time ring.

Demographics

Population, households and median household income in the trade area. Tenants screen sites on these.

Traffic countsVPD

Vehicles per day passing the site. Pads want 25,000+ VPD on the main road.

Access & visibility

Signalized intersections, curb cuts, turn lanes and pylon signage. Hard to fix after the fact.

Parking ratio

Spaces per 1,000 SF of GLA, typically 4–5. Excess parking can become pad sites.

Grocer sales per SF

A strong grocer does $600–1,000+/SF. It shows how much traffic the anchor brings.

Foot-traffic data

Mobile location data (e.g. Placer.ai) showing visits, dwell time and where shoppers come from.

05Valuation & credit

Anchor vs. shop rent

Anchors pay maybe $8–18/SF on long leases; shops pay $25–45/SF on shorter ones. Value depends heavily on shop occupancy.

Dark anchor risk

An anchor closing can trigger co-tenancy, cut traffic and cause shop tenants to leave. The single biggest retail risk.

Box split / demising

Dividing a large vacant box into smaller units for junior anchors.

Re-anchoring

Replacing a failed anchor with a stronger traffic driver, often a grocer, fitness or medical use.

Densification

Adding pads or residential on excess parking. Long-term upside on large retail sites.

Lender focus

Anchor lease term vs. loan term, co-tenancy exposure, tenant sales and rollover. Many lenders require anchors to extend past loan maturity.

No retail terms match that filter.

A regional grocer has signed a 20-year lease. Plan: a 100,000 SF center with the grocer, a junior anchor, in-line shops, and four pad sites.

Case 2 · Distressed acquisition, reposition & long-term hold

280,000 SF community center

IC memo · live model

A 1990s community center on 28 acres at a busy suburban intersection. Two anchors went bankrupt, leaving a 60,000 SF and a 45,000 SF box dark. Co-tenancy clauses let several shop tenants cut their rent, and the center is now 55% leased. The CMBS loan defaulted and the special servicer is selling the property. Our plan is to re-anchor, lease up, and hold it long term for steady cash flow.

Step 1Is the real estate still good?

  • Trade area: 120,000 people within 5 miles and growing; the closest grocery-anchored competitor is 3 miles away.
  • Traffic: 45,000 vehicles per day on the main road, signalized access, strong visibility.
  • The failure was tenant-specific: the anchors were weak national chains that went bankrupt, not a sign that the location stopped working.
  • Excess land: the parking field is far larger than needed, which allows new pad sites.

Step 2In-place financials

$M

Step 3The reposition plan

  1. Re-anchor with a grocer. Split the 60,000 SF box into a 45,000 SF grocer and a 15,000 SF urgent care / medical tenant.
  2. Re-tenant the 45,000 SF box as a 30,000 SF fitness club plus a 15,000 SF off-price retailer.
  3. Cure co-tenancy. Once the grocer opens, shop tenants go back to full rent.
  4. Create 3 pad sites on excess parking for a drive-thru QSR, coffee and a bank, all on ground leases.
  5. Refresh the property: new facades, pylon signage, LED lighting and a resurfaced lot.
  6. Lease remaining shops to service, food and medical tenants that resist e-commerce.

Step 4All-in basis

Line item$MPer SF

Step 5Stabilized NOI

TenancySFRent$M

Step 6Long-term hold: refinance instead of selling

The goal is steady cash flow, so at stabilization we replace the bridge loan with long-term fixed-rate debt and keep the asset.

Refinance at stabilizationValue

Holding gives up some IRR for a much bigger equity multiple and years of predictable cash. That trade fits a long-term owner such as a family office, a REIT or your own future platform. What makes the long hold work:

  • Long anchor term. The grocer's 20-year lease runs past the loan maturity, which lenders want to see.
  • Necessity tenant mix. Grocery, medical, fitness, food and services are less exposed to e-commerce.
  • Built-in growth. 3% shop bumps, percentage rent from strong tenants, and mark-to-market as older shop leases roll.
  • Future options. More pads, or residential on the remaining excess parking, years from now.
What moves the dealNOISell IRRHold IRRHold multiple

Step 7Retail-specific diligence

  • Co-tenancy: which tenants have rights, the cure period, and what counts as "replacement anchor."
  • REA: do anchors or other owners hold approval rights over pads, new uses or site plan changes? This can block the plan.
  • Exclusives: an existing pharmacy or gym exclusive may stop you from signing the medical or fitness tenant.
  • Dark-but-paying leases: confirm whether the bankrupt anchors rejected their leases in bankruptcy or still control the boxes.
  • Tenant sales and occupancy cost ratios for every tenant that reports.
  • Environmental: former dry cleaners and gas stations are the classic retail contamination risk.
  • CAM audit: under-billed recoveries are both a risk and an upside.
Credit lensA bridge lender sizes off the business plan and holds TI and capex as future funding, released as leases are signed. The permanent lender then focuses on anchor lease term relative to the loan, co-tenancy exposure and the share of income from national vs. local tenants.

Case 3 · Distressed acquisition, re-anchor & sell

150,000 SF neighborhood center with a dark grocer box

IC memo · live model

A 1980s neighborhood center on 16 acres in a dense, middle-income suburb. Its grocer closed after a chain merger, leaving a 55,000 SF box dark. Shop tenants used co-tenancy clauses to cut their rent, and the center is now 38% leased. The owner is out of money and the lender wants out. Unlike Case 2, our plan is a merchant strategy: fix it fast, then sell to a long-term buyer.

Step 1Why sell instead of hold?

  • The profit is created up front. We buy at a deep discount and re-anchor. Once the grocer is open, a core buyer will pay a much lower cap rate than we paid.
  • IRR falls the longer we hold. After stabilization, the remaining return is a steady ~7% yield, which is below our fund's target.
  • Fund life. Value-add funds typically need to return capital in 3–5 years.
  • Deep buyer pool. Grocery-anchored centers are in demand from REITs, private buyers and 1031 exchange buyers.

Step 2In-place financials

$M

Step 3The plan

  1. Sign a new grocer before closing, or at least a signed letter of intent. A 54,000 SF grocer on a 15-year lease at $12 NNN, with $60/SF of landlord work.
  2. Cure co-tenancy so existing shops return to full rent once the grocer opens.
  3. Lease 25,000 SF of shops at $22 to service, food and medical tenants.
  4. Create and sell two pad sites for a drive-thru QSR and a bank at ~$1.6M each. Selling (rather than ground-leasing) returns capital early.
  5. Refresh the property: facade, signage, lighting and parking lot.
  6. Prepare the sale as soon as the grocer has been open long enough to show sales.

Step 4All-in basis

Line item$M

Step 5Stabilized NOI

TenancySFRent$M

Step 6The sale

What buyers want to see before paying a core priceThe grocer open and reporting sales (ideally 6–12 months), signed estoppels from every major tenant, a clean CAM reconciliation, co-tenancy cured, and a long anchor term. Selling before these are in place means a higher cap rate and a lower price.

Step 7Timing the exit

Sell when...MonthCapPriceLevered IRRMultiple

Selling earlier returns capital sooner but at a higher cap rate; waiting for sales data earns the core price. Holding long term is Case 2: lower IRR, more total profit.

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer.

Q1Why would a landlord accept $14/SF from a grocer when shops pay $36?

Show answer

The grocer creates the weekly traffic that makes every other tenant viable. Without it, shop occupancy and rents fall and pads lose appeal. The grocer's rent is effectively a marketing cost the landlord recovers through higher shop and pad rents.

Q2An anchor goes dark but keeps paying rent. Why is NOI still at risk?

Show answer

Traffic drops, and co-tenancy clauses keyed to that anchor may let shop tenants cut their rent or terminate. Shops then see lower sales and may not renew. Rent from the anchor continues on paper while income from everyone else erodes.

Q3A shop tenant has $350/SF of sales and pays $36 rent plus $10 of CAM, taxes and insurance. Is that healthy?

Show answer

Occupancy cost is $46 ÷ $350 = 13.1%, at the top of the comfortable range for most shop tenants. It can probably pay, but a rent increase at renewal is risky. Check the tenant's trend in sales and its category norms in the calculator.

Q4In Case 2, why might you refinance and hold instead of selling at stabilization?

Show answer

Refinancing returns much of the equity while you keep a stabilized, grocery-anchored asset with long leases and growing cash flow. The IRR is a bit lower than selling, but the equity multiple and total dollars earned are much higher, and you avoid transaction costs and reinvestment risk.

01The care continuum

Senior housing is sorted by how much care residents need. More care means higher rates, more staff, more regulation and thinner margins.

Active adult (55+)

Age-restricted rental apartments with amenities but no services or care. Underwritten much like multifamily.

MF analog Closest to a normal apartment

Independent livingIL

Apartments for seniors (often 75+) with services bundled into rent: meals, housekeeping, transport, activities. Usually not licensed.

Assisted livingAL

Help with activities of daily living (bathing, dressing, medication). State-licensed, 24-hour staff.

Memory careMC

Secured units for residents with dementia. Highest staffing and rates outside nursing homes.

Skilled nursingSNF

Nursing homes providing medical care. Paid largely by Medicare and Medicaid, so it's a healthcare business with heavy regulation.

CCRC / Life plan community

Campus offering IL, AL, MC and often nursing, so residents can age in place. Often uses entrance fees.

Acuity

How much care a resident needs. Higher acuity means more staff hours and higher fees.

Activities of daily livingADLs

Bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, transferring, continence. Needing help with 2+ usually qualifies for AL.

02Revenue

Monthly rate / base rent

The monthly charge for the unit and bundled services, e.g. $4,500 IL or $7,000 AL.

Level of care fees

Extra monthly charges by care tier or points, added to base rent in AL.

Community fee

One-time move-in fee in rental communities, often equal to about one month's rent.

Entrance fee

Large upfront payment in CCRCs ($200k–$1M+), sometimes partly refundable, plus lower monthly fees.

Private pay

Residents pay from savings, home sale proceeds or long-term care insurance. Most IL, AL and MC is private pay.

RevPOR

Revenue per occupied room (unit) per month. The senior housing version of ADR.

MF analog Average rent per occupied unit

Second-person fee

Extra monthly charge when a couple shares a unit.

Length of stay

Roughly 2–4 years in IL, ~2 years in AL, under 2 years in MC. Turnover is constant, so marketing never stops.

Move-ins / move-outs

Net move-ins per month drive lease-up. A new community might add 3–5 net residents a month.

03Operations & structures

Operator

The company that runs the community, hires staff and delivers care. Operator quality drives value as much as location.

Labor ratio

Labor as a share of revenue or expenses, often 50–60% of operating costs. The biggest risk in the P&L.

Agency labor

Temporary staff from agencies at premium rates. A warning sign when it's high.

Management fee

Operator's fee, typically ~5% of revenue, sometimes with incentives.

Operating margin

Roughly 35–45% for IL, 25–35% for AL and MC. Apartments run 55–65%.

RIDEA structure

Lets a REIT own the operating business through a taxable subsidiary and keep the profits, with an operator under a management contract. The owner takes operating risk and upside.

Triple-net lease to operator

Owner leases the whole building to an operator for fixed rent. Owner gets steady income; operator takes the business risk.

Rent coverage (EBITDAR)

Operator's earnings before rent ÷ rent owed. Measures whether a NNN-leased operator can keep paying.

Licensing

States license AL and MC, with rules on staffing, training, building features and inspections.

04Market & underwriting

Primary market areaPMA

Where most residents come from, often 5–10 miles. Adult children nearby often choose the community.

Age- & income-qualified households

Seniors in the PMA old enough (75+ for AL, 80+ for MC) and wealthy enough (income plus home equity) to pay.

Penetration rate

Existing and planned units ÷ qualified households. High penetration means the market is saturated.

Capture rate

Share of qualified households this project must attract to fill. Lower is safer.

NIC MAP

Industry data source for senior housing occupancy, rates and supply by market.

Lease-up period

Typically 24–36 months to reach ~90% occupancy. Requires a large operating deficit reserve.

HUD 232

Government-insured long-term loan program for stabilized senior housing and nursing homes. A common take-out for construction loans.

No senior living terms match that filter.

Senior living · Case 1 · New construction

120-unit assisted living & memory care

IC memo · illustrative

A 6-acre site in an affluent suburb near a hospital. The 80+ population within 7 miles is growing about 4% a year, and almost no new senior housing has been built since 2020. Plan: a 120-unit community with 90 assisted living and 30 memory care units, run by an experienced third-party operator.

Step 1Market feasibility

  • Qualified demand: ~3,200 households aged 75+ with enough income and home equity to pay ~$8,000+/month.
  • Penetration: existing AL/MC supply plus this project is ~11% of qualified households. Under ~15% is typically considered healthy.
  • Capture rate: we need to fill ~110 units, about 3–4% of qualified households.
  • Competition: nearby communities are older, 90%+ occupied and raising rates.

Senior living · Case 2 · Conversion

140-unit apartment building → independent living

IC memo · illustrative

A 2000-built, 4-story, 140-unit apartment building with elevators and interior corridors, in an affluent suburb near a hospital. New Class A apartments nearby are pulling renters away, so occupancy is 85% and rents are flat. Meanwhile the area has deep 75+ demand and no independent living. Plan: buy it and convert it to independent living with services.

Step 1Why independent living, not assisted living?

  • No license needed in most states. IL bundles hospitality services, not care. Residents can hire home health aides separately.
  • The building works as is: elevators, interior corridors and an accessible ground floor. AL would require institutional building codes, wider corridors, nurse call systems and more sprinklers.
  • Lower operating risk: far fewer staff than AL.
Building checklist for conversionElevators to every floor, interior (not breezeway) corridors, ground-floor space for dining and a commercial kitchen, unit bathrooms that can take walk-in showers, and enough parking. Many garden-style apartment buildings fail this test.

$M

Operating expenses (~45%)(1.23)

Purchase price: $24.0M ($171k/unit), a 6.3% cap on in-place NOI.

Step 3Conversion plan & budget

  1. Convert 12 ground-floor units (~12,000 SF) into a dining room, commercial kitchen, wellness room, library and activity space. 128 units remain.
  2. Upgrade units for aging in place: walk-in showers, grab bars, lever handles, better lighting, emergency call pendants.
  3. Add a generator, upgrade elevators and fix accessibility gaps.
  4. Hire an IL operator for dining, housekeeping, transport, activities and marketing.
  5. Convert through natural turnover: existing residents stay until their leases end (see legal notes below).

New-build IL in this market would cost $450k+ per unit, so the conversion delivers the product at about two-thirds of new cost.

Step 6Legal & execution risks

  • Fair housing: you can't push out current residents because of age. Convert through lease expirations and voluntary moves, and get counsel on any age-restriction plan.
  • Age restriction (HOPA): a 55+ designation requires at least 80% of occupied units to have a resident 55 or older, plus published policies and age verification.
  • Stay out of care: if staff start helping with medications or bathing, the building may need an AL license.
  • Zoning & code: a commercial kitchen and dining room may need approvals, grease and ventilation upgrades.
  • Lease-up: IL fills at maybe 2–4 net move-ins a month, slower than apartments. Some residents may decide not to stay.
  • Operator: choose one with IL conversion experience and strong local marketing to adult children.
Credit lensA lender will underwrite the transition as a lease-up with a business-plan risk. Expect a bridge loan with future funding for capex, an interest reserve, and a requirement for an experienced operator. The take-out comes from agency or bank seniors housing lenders after 12+ months of stabilized operations.

Physical vs. economic occupancy

A facility can be 90% full and still lose money to discounts and old below-market rents. Economic occupancy = rent actually collected ÷ rent at street rates if 100% full.

01Product

Net rentable SFNRSF

The unit floor area customers rent. Storage is priced and measured per NRSF.

MF analog Net rentable area

Gross-to-net efficiency

NRSF ÷ gross building SF. ~75–80% in multi-story buildings with hallways and elevators; ~90%+ for single-story drive-up.

Climate-controlledCC

Heated and cooled interior units. Rents for more and is the standard in new multi-story facilities.

Drive-up / non-climate

Single-story units with roll-up doors you can drive to. Cheaper to build, lower rent.

Unit mix

Sizes from 5×5 to 10×30. 10×10s are the benchmark unit; small units earn the most per SF.

Boat / RV storage

Covered or open parking spaces for vehicles. Low capex, strong demand in some suburbs and resort areas.

Conversion

Turning a vacant big-box store, warehouse or office into storage.

02Revenue

Street rate / web rate

The advertised rate for a new customer today. Changes daily with demand, like hotel rates.

In-place rent

What existing customers are paying, often different from street rate.

Physical occupancy

Rented NRSF (or units) ÷ total. Stabilized facilities run ~88–93%.

Economic occupancy

Actual rent collected ÷ potential rent at street rates if fully leased. Captures discounts and below-market rents.

ECRI

Existing customer rate increases. Raising rents on current customers, often 8–15% a year after move-in. A major profit driver because few people move out over a small increase.

Move-in specials

Low teaser rates such as "first month $1" to win new customers, recovered later through ECRIs.

Tenant protection / insurance

Coverage sold to customers for their stored goods. High-margin ancillary income.

Ancillary income

Locks, boxes, truck rental, admin and late fees.

Length of stay

Many customers stay over a year, which is why ECRIs work.

Seasonality

Demand peaks in late spring and summer with moving season.

03Demand & supply

Trade area

Usually a 3-mile radius (5+ miles in rural areas). Most customers come from close by.

SF per capita

Storage NRSF in the trade area ÷ population. The U.S. averages around 7–8 SF; well above that suggests oversupply.

Demand drivers

The "4 Ds" (death, divorce, dislocation, downsizing), plus moves, apartment living and small businesses.

Supply pipeline

New facilities planned or under construction in the trade area. Storage is quick to build, so supply can arrive fast.

Lease-up

New facilities take ~3–4 years to stabilize, filling with discounts and then pushing rates.

04Operations & investment

NOI margin

Roughly 60–70% at stabilization. Few staff, little maintenance, no unit turns.

MF analog MF runs ~55–65%

Third-party management

Large platforms run facilities for owners for ~6% of revenue, bringing pricing software, websites and brand.

Revenue management

Software that sets street rates and ECRIs by unit type based on demand.

Mom-and-pop

Independent owner-operators. Often under-priced, under-marketed and without ECRI programs: the classic value-add target.

Lien sale / auction

Legal process to sell a delinquent customer's goods after notice.

CO deal

A developer agrees to sell a new facility to a buyer (often a REIT) when it receives its certificate of occupancy, at a pre-set price, before lease-up.

Expansion phase

Building more units on excess land at an existing facility. Cheap growth with proven demand.

Price per NRSF

How storage assets are compared, alongside cap rate.

No self-storage terms match that filter.

Self-storage · Case 1 · New construction

78,000 NRSF climate-controlled facility

IC memo · illustrative

A 2-acre site on a busy arterial road in an infill suburb. 120,000 people live within 3 miles, with lots of apartment renters and new home sales. Existing supply is ~5.5 SF per person and no new facilities are planned nearby. Plan: a 3-story, 100,000 GSF climate-controlled building with 78,000 NRSF.

Step 1Feasibility

  • Supply: 5.5 SF per capita vs. ~7–8 national average, so the area is underserved.
  • Demand: high renter share, steady home turnover, and growth in small businesses.
  • Visibility: storage is an impulse-and-convenience purchase, so a site on a road people pass daily is key.
  • Rates: competitors' 10×10 climate-controlled units rent for ~$215–230/month.

Self-storage · Case 2 · Value-add

62,000 NRSF mom-and-pop facility + expansion

IC memo · illustrative

A 1998 single-story drive-up facility on 6 acres, owned by its original family. It's 78% occupied with in-place rents about 25% below street rates. There's no website, no online rentals, no rate increase program and no tenant protection plan. Two of the acres are unused.

Step 1Where the value is

  • Revenue management: street rates haven't moved in years, and existing customers never get rate increases.
  • Marketing: no website or online rentals in a business where most customers search on their phone.
  • Ancillary income: no tenant protection plan or merchandise sales.
  • Excess land: room for a 20,000 NRSF climate-controlled building where demand already exists.

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer.

Q1Why do assisted living margins run ~30–35% when apartments run ~60%?

Show answer

The owner pays for 24-hour care staff, meals, housekeeping, activities and licensing compliance. Labor alone can be over a third of revenue. Rates are much higher per unit, but most of the extra revenue goes to delivering services.

Q2What makes an apartment building a good candidate for independent living conversion?

Show answer

Elevators, interior corridors, ground-floor space for dining and a commercial kitchen, bathrooms that can be made accessible, a location near healthcare in an affluent area with strong 75+ demand, and weak apartment fundamentals that make the conversion worth the operating risk.

Q3A storage facility is 90% physically occupied but 70% economically occupied. What does that tell you?

Show answer

Customers are paying well below street rates, through discounts, old rents or no rate increase program. That's an opportunity if street rates are real: an ECRI program and better revenue management can raise income without adding a single customer.

Q4Why might a storage developer sell at certificate of occupancy instead of leasing up?

Show answer

Lease-up takes ~3 years and is exposed to new competing supply. Selling at CO to a REIT locks in a price, returns capital in about a year and gives a higher IRR, even though total profit is lower than selling a stabilized facility.

Q5As a lender, what's the first thing you'd ask about a senior living deal that you wouldn't ask about an apartment deal?

Show answer

Who the operator is and how they've performed: occupancy and margins at their other communities, staffing and agency use, state survey and licensing history. In senior living, the operator's execution matters as much as the building.

Core concept · Capital markets

CMBS

Commercial mortgages pooled into a trust and sold as bonds. Each buyer owns a different slice of the same loans: cash flows from the top, losses from the bottom.

Typical conduit
$700M–1.2B, 30–60 loans
Loan term
10-yr fixed, often IO
Key loan metric
Debt yield
Protection
Subordination
Risk retention
5%, held 5 years
In charge of workouts
Special servicer

Loan sizing check

The three numbers every CMBS buyer quotes first. Lenders size the loan to whichever test is tightest.

–

–

01Deal types

Conduit

A pool of 30–60 fixed-rate loans from several lenders, diversified by property type and geography. The classic CMBS deal.

Single-asset single-borrowerSASB

One large loan (or one portfolio) securitized on its own. Buyers underwrite one property and sponsor in depth.

CRE CLO

Pools of floating-rate transitional (bridge) loans, often actively managed. Sponsor retains the bottom slice.

Agency CMBS

Multifamily loans securitized by Freddie Mac (K-deals) or Fannie Mae (DUS). Senior bonds carry the agency's guarantee.

Pari passu split loan

A large loan cut into equal-priority notes placed in several conduits. One deal's servicing agreement controls the whole loan.

Mezzanine loan

A loan secured by the borrower's ownership interest, sitting outside the trust and subordinate to the mortgage.

02Structure

Tranche / class

A slice of the bond stack with its own rating, size, coupon and priority (Class A-1, A-S, B, C, D...).

Credit enhancementCE

The share of the pool below a tranche that must be lost before it loses a dollar. A senior AAA might have 30%.

Attachment / detachment

The pool-loss levels where a tranche starts and finishes taking losses. A BBB- tranche might attach at 8% and detach at 10.5%.

Sequential pay

Principal pays the most senior class first until it's retired, then the next. Losses hit the most junior class first.

Interest-only stripX class

A bond that receives excess interest but no principal. Hurt by early payoffs and defaults.

WAC

Weighted average coupon of the loans in the pool. Some bond coupons are tied to it.

REMIC

The tax election that lets the trust pass income to bondholders without entity tax. It strictly limits what the trust can do with loans, including modifications.

Risk retention

Rule requiring 5% of the deal's credit risk to be kept for 5 years, usually by a third-party B-piece buyer holding the bottom classes.

B-piece buyer

Investor that buys the unrated and low-rated bottom classes, re-underwrites every loan and usually controls special servicing.

03Parties & documents

Pooling & servicing agreementPSA

The deal's governing contract: who does what, how cash flows, how decisions get made.

Master servicer

Collects payments from performing loans, sends reports and advances missed payments if it expects to recover them.

Special servicer

Takes over loans in default or at risk of default and decides how to resolve them. Paid fees on workouts and liquidations.

Directing certificateholder / controlling class

The most junior class that still has enough value (usually the B-piece). Can appoint and replace the special servicer and consent to major decisions.

Operating advisor

Independent party that reviews the special servicer's actions on behalf of all bondholders.

Trustee / certificate administrator

Holds the loans for the trust and calculates and pays distributions to bondholders.

Rating agencies

Moody's, S&P, Fitch, KBRA, DBRS Morningstar. Each applies its own haircuts to NCF and value to size credit enhancement.

Annex A

The loan-by-loan data tape in the offering documents: balances, NCF, DSCR, LTV, tenants, reserves.

04Loan terms

Underwritten NCFUW NCF

Net cash flow after reserves for TI, LC and capex, as underwritten by the lender. The basis for every metric.

MF analog NOI less replacement reserves

Debt yield

NCF ÷ loan. Independent of interest rate and amortization, so it's the purest test of leverage. ~9–11% is typical for conduit loans.

Non-recourse & carve-outs

The borrower isn't personally liable except for "bad acts" such as fraud, unauthorized transfers or voluntary bankruptcy, backed by a guarantor.

SPE / bankruptcy-remote

The borrower is a single-purpose entity owning only the property, often with an independent director.

Defeasance

Prepayment substitute: the borrower buys Treasuries that replicate the loan's payments, freeing the property. Keeps bondholders whole.

Yield maintenance

A prepayment penalty that makes the lender whole for lost interest at current rates.

Lockout / open period

Lockout: no prepayment at all. Open period: the final months when the loan can be repaid at par.

Lockbox & cash management

Rents go into a lender-controlled account. "Springing" cash management starts only after a trigger such as low DSCR or a major tenant leaving.

Cash sweep / trap

Excess cash is held as extra reserves instead of going to the borrower once a trigger hits.

Balloon / refi risk

Most conduit loans don't amortize much, so the full balance must be refinanced at maturity.

05Surveillance & distress

Watchlist

Loans flagged by the master servicer for low DSCR, big rollover, occupancy loss or other issues.

Term vs. maturity default

Term default: can't pay during the loan. Maturity default: pays fine but can't refinance at the end. Recent office distress is mostly maturity default.

Servicing transfer

Moving a loan from the master servicer to the special servicer after default, imminent default or a borrower request.

P&I advances

The master servicer keeps paying bondholders on a delinquent loan as long as it expects to recover the money from the property.

Nonrecoverability

The servicer's decision that advances can't be recovered, so they stop. Bottom classes then miss interest.

Appraisal reduction amountARA

Roughly: loan balance plus unpaid amounts minus 90% of the new appraised value. Reduces advances and can shift control of the deal.

ASER

Appraisal subordinate entitlement reduction: interest on the appraisal-reduced portion is not advanced, so the lowest classes take an interest shortfall.

Control appraisal period / appraised out

When ARAs shrink the controlling class below 25% of its original balance, control passes to the next class up.

Loss severity

Loss ÷ loan balance at liquidation, including advances and fees. Historical CMBS averages are roughly 35–50%.

Modification / A-B split

Changing loan terms. An A/B (hope note) split keeps a performing A-note and a B-note paid only if value recovers.

Discounted payoffDPO

The special servicer accepts less than the full balance to settle the loan.

REO

Real estate owned by the trust after foreclosure or deed-in-lieu, then sold.

No CMBS terms match that filter.

A conduit deal from first borrower call to final bond payment. Steps A–I usually take 3–6 months from loan application to bond closing; J–L run for the next ~10 years. Times are typical ranges and vary by deal and market conditions.

A

Origination1–3 weeks

Borrower asks a conduit lender (an investment bank or other loan seller) for a fixed-rate loan. Lender issues a term sheet sized to the tightest of debt yield, DSCR and LTV, and takes a deposit.

B

Underwriting30–60 days

Appraisal, property condition report, Phase I environmental, seismic and zoning reports, site visit, rent roll and lease audit, sponsor background checks. Lender sets UW NCF, reserves and cash management triggers.

C

Loan closing1–2 weeks

Borrower is set up as an SPE. Loan closes with a carve-out guaranty, lockbox, upfront reserves (taxes, insurance, TI/LC, deferred maintenance), and prepayment terms (lockout, then defeasance).

D

Warehouse1–6 months

The loan sits on the lender's balance sheet, usually interest-rate hedged, until enough loans are gathered. Market moves during this time are the lender's risk.

E

Pool aggregation1–3 months (overlaps warehouse)

Several loan sellers combine loans into one pool. The deal team checks diversity by property type, geography, sponsor and loan size.

F

Rating agencies4–8 weeks

Two or three agencies re-underwrite the pool with their own NCF haircuts and cap rates, then tell the issuer how much subordination each rating needs.

G

B-piece review & kick-outs3–5 weeks (overlaps ratings)

The B-piece buyer re-underwrites every loan and can demand that weak loans be removed ("kicked out") or the price of their bonds be cut. This is where the deal's real credit work happens.

H

Structuring, marketing & pricing1–2 weeks

Banks set class sizes, publish the preliminary prospectus and Annex A, agencies release pre-sale reports, investors ask questions, then bonds price at spreads over swaps and are allocated.

I

Closing & trust formation~1–2 weeks after pricing

Loans transfer into the REMIC trust. The PSA names the trustee, certificate administrator, master servicer, special servicer, operating advisor and directing certificateholder.

J

Monthly servicing & surveillanceLife of the loans, ~10 years

Master servicer collects payments, reports in a standard industry format, and watchlists problem loans. Investors track performance through data services like Trepp.

K

Special servicing (if needed)1–3+ years per loan

Defaulted or at-risk loans transfer to the special servicer for a workout. See the flowcharts tab.

L

Payoff, defeasance or liquidationMostly around year 10; trust winds down after

Loans defease, refinance at maturity, or are worked out. Principal pays down the stack sequentially, losses are allocated from the bottom up, and the trust winds down when the last loan resolves.

Once a loan is in trouble, the special servicer must pick the option with the highest net present value for all bondholders as a whole, not for any one class.

3. Where cash goes, and where losses go

Cash: top down each month
Loan payments (plus advances)
Servicing & trustee fees
Interest to each class, senior first
Principal to Class A until paid off, then A-S, B, C...
Losses: bottom up
