Then B- (G), BB- (F)
Then BBB- (E), BBB (D)...
AAA only after ~30% of the pool is lost
Why special servicers are controversialThe special servicer is often affiliated with the B-piece buyer, who loses first. Extending a loan delays losses that would hit the B-piece today, even if a sale now would be better for senior bonds. The operating advisor and the "whole trust" NPV standard exist to check that conflict.

Case study · Conduit loan analysis

$80M loan on a 400,000 SF suburban office campus

Illustrative

This loan is the 4th-largest in a $1.0 billion conduit with 45 loans. Everyone in the stack sees the same Annex A line, but each buyer asks a different question: the AAA buyer asks "how bad would things have to get?", while the B-piece buyer asks "what will this specific building be worth in year 10?"

Step 1The loan

Property400,000 SF Class A suburban office, 91% leased, WALT 5.8 years
Largest tenant112,000 SF (28%), investment-grade, lease expires in year 6 of the loan
Loan$80M, 10-year fixed 6.40%, interest-only full term
Prepayment2-year lockout, then defeasance; open the last 3 months
Reserves$4M upfront TI/LC; $1.00/SF per year ongoing
Cash managementSpringing: sweep starts if DSCR < 1.25x or the large tenant gives notice or goes dark
SponsorInstitutional fund; non-recourse with carve-out guaranty
Lender viewRating agency view
NCF$8.0M$7.2M (10% haircut)
Cap rate6.0% (appraisal)8.25% (agency)
Value$133M$87.3M
LTV60%92%
Debt yield10.0%9.0%
DSCR (IO)1.56x1.41x

The agency's 92% LTV, not the lender's 60%, drives how much subordination this loan requires. Agencies assume through-the-cycle cap rates and haircut cash flow.

Step 2The bond stack and where a loss lands

Move the slider to see which classes are written down at a given cumulative pool loss. Each 1% of pool loss is $10M.

ClassRatingSizeCEWritten down

Step 3The stress scenario every buyer runs

  1. In year 6 the large tenant leaves. The cash sweep has trapped ~$4M by then to help re-lease.
  2. Re-leasing is slow. By maturity, the building is 75% leased with NCF of $6.2M.
  3. At an 8.5% cap rate, value at maturity is ~$72.9M. A new lender needs a 10% debt yield, so the most it will lend is ~$62M.
  4. The borrower can't refinance the $80M balance: maturity default.
  5. The special servicer orders a new appraisal. ARA = $80M + ~$2M unpaid amounts − 90% × $72.9M ≈ $16.4M.
  6. ASER: interest on that $16.4M (~$1.05M a year) is no longer advanced, so the unrated class takes an interest shortfall.
  7. If liquidated: ~$66M net recovery after costs and repaying advances, so a ~$18M loss (~22% severity), or 1.8% of the pool.

Step 4How each buyer analyzes this loan

Senior AAAClass A · CE 30%

Insurers, banks, pension funds, money managers

Focus: the pool, not the loan. Total office exposure, top-10 concentration, share of IO loans, agency LTV, and extension risk (getting repaid later than expected).

This loan: barely matters. Losses would need to exceed 30% of the pool before Class A loses a dollar, many times worse than the 2008 crisis.

Expects: ~swaps + 95–115 bps

Junior AAA (A-S)CE ~22%

Insurers and money managers wanting extra spread at AAA

Focus: same pool view, plus how thin the cushion below them is and whether the class could be downgraded.

This loan: a line item in the office concentration analysis.

Expects: ~swaps + 130–160 bps

AA / AClasses B–C · CE 13.5–17.5%

Insurers, crossover funds

Focus: the 10–15 largest loans and the sectors under stress. They run scenarios where all office loans default at high severities.

This loan: 8% of the pool and office, so it's in every stress case. They check the year-6 rollover and the cash sweep.

Expects: ~swaps + 170–280 bps

BBB / BBB-Classes D–E · CE 8–10.5%

Hedge funds, credit funds, some insurers and CDO/CLO buyers

Focus: loan-by-loan underwriting of the top 20+ loans. Downgrade risk matters because many holders can't keep bonds that fall below investment grade.

This loan: a key driver. If 4–5 loans like it fail, BBB- is hit. They model the maturity default and ask what an office buyer will pay in year 10.

Expects: ~swaps + 350–500 bps

BB / BClasses F–G · CE 3.5–5.5%

Usually the B-piece buyer as part of its 5% retention; some high-yield funds

Focus: every loan. With only 3.5–5.5% below them, two or three large failures cause losses.

This loan: three loans like it (5.4% loss) wipe out the unrated class and nearly all of Class G.

Expects: ~swaps + 700–1,300 bps

Unrated (B-piece)Class H · first loss

Specialized B-piece investors, often with an affiliated special servicer

Focus: full re-underwriting before pricing: site visits, their own NCF and value for each loan, sponsor reputation. They kick out loans they don't like.

This loan: they might cut NCF to ~$7.4M, give the large tenant a 50% renewal probability, and demand a lower price or a smaller loan. One liquidation (~$18M) erases about half of the $35M class.

Expects: ~15–20% unlevered yield, bought at a deep discount; plus control of special servicing

Spreads are illustrative ranges for a recent conduit and move constantly. Check current pricing before quoting them.

Step 5Control and conflicts in the stress case

The $16.4M ARA is applied to the unrated class: $35M − $16.4M = $18.6M, or 53% of its original balance. That's still above the 25% threshold, so the B-piece keeps control of the deal.

The B-piece's affiliated special servicer may prefer a 2–3 year extension: the loss isn't realized yet, and the building might recover. Senior holders may prefer a sale now, before value falls further. The operating advisor reviews whether the chosen path really maximizes value for all bondholders.

Credit career angleFirms like special servicers, B-piece buyers and CMBS credit funds do exactly this work: re-underwriting loans at origination, watching surveillance data, and running workouts. Knowing each tranche's perspective is what interviewers test.

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer.

Q1Why do CMBS lenders focus on debt yield rather than DSCR?

Show answer

DSCR changes with the interest rate and amortization, so a low rate or an IO period can make a risky loan look safe. Debt yield (NCF ÷ loan) ignores the loan's terms and shows how much cash the property produces relative to the debt, which is what a buyer at maturity or after foreclosure will care about.

Q2A loan has 1.60x DSCR today but a 7.5% debt yield. What's the risk?

Show answer

Refinance risk. The DSCR is high because the coupon is low, but a new lender at maturity will likely require 9–10% debt yield. At 7.5%, the borrower would need to pay down 20–25% of the loan to refinance, which can lead to a maturity default.

Q3Why does the B-piece buyer get to control special servicing?

Show answer

It's first in line for losses, so it has the strongest incentive to manage problem loans well, and it did the deepest underwriting. The trade-off is a conflict of interest, which is why control shifts up the stack once appraisal reductions wipe out most of its class, and why an operating advisor reviews decisions.

Q4What happens to the bottom class's monthly interest when an appraisal reduction is applied?

Show answer

Under ASER, the master servicer advances interest only on the loan balance net of the ARA. The missing interest becomes a shortfall that hits the most junior classes first, so they lose cash flow before any principal loss is realized.

Q5A BBB- class attaches at 8%. The pool has 12% office loans. What would you want to know?

Show answer

The specific office loans: size, debt yield, rollover before maturity, tenant credit, location, and reserves. Then a stress case: if half of them default at 40–50% severity, pool losses would be ~2.5–3%. Add expected losses from other sectors and compare the total to the 8% attachment, and check how close the class sits to a downgrade.

Multifamily · From the beginning

Multifamily

Hundreds of one-year leases to individual households. Demand is steady because everyone needs a home, so returns come from rent growth, tight operations and buying or building at the right basis.

Priced per
Unit (and per SF)
Lease
~12 months

~55–65%
Favorite lender
Fannie Mae / Freddie Mac
For-sale cousin
Condominiums

Rent roll to value

The basic apartment pro forma: start from potential rent, subtract vacancy and losses, add other income, subtract expenses, and divide by a cap rate.

EGI

01Product types

Garden-style

2–4 story walk-up buildings on a large suburban site with surface parking. Cheapest to build per unit.

Mid-rise / podium ("5-over-1")

4–7 stories of wood frame over a concrete podium with parking or retail. The most common new urban and suburban product.

Wrap

Apartments wrapped around a central parking garage.

High-rise

Concrete or steel towers, usually 10+ stories. Highest cost per unit, highest rents.

Build-to-rentBTR

Single-family homes or townhomes built as a rental community.

Class A / B / C

A: new, top amenities and rents. B: 10–30 years old, solid. C: older, dated, lower rents, often more operating problems.

Vintage

The year built. "1970s vintage" signals older systems and likely capex needs.

Affordable / LIHTC

Rents restricted to households under income limits, usually funded with Low-Income Housing Tax Credits.

Workforce housing

Rents affordable to middle-income households (roughly 60–120% of area median income), often unregulated Class B and C.

Rent-stabilized

Units where rent increases are capped by law (e.g. much of NYC's older stock). Limits upside and value-add options.

Condo vs. co-op

Condo: you own your unit and a share of common areas. Co-op: you own shares in a corporation that owns the building. Both are for-sale housing, not rentals.

02Revenue

Gross potential rentGPR

Rent if every unit were leased at market rent for the full year.

Market rent vs. in-place rent

Market: what a new tenant would pay today. In-place: what current tenants actually pay.

Loss-to-lease

The gap between market rent and in-place rent. Shrinks as leases renew at higher rates.

Physical vs. economic occupancy

Physical: share of units with a tenant. Economic: share of potential rent actually collected after vacancy, concessions and bad debt.

Concessions

Free rent or discounts to sign a lease, e.g. "6 weeks free" during lease-up.

Bad debt / delinquency

Rent owed but not collected. A big issue in Class C and in some markets with slow eviction courts.

Other income

Parking, pet rent, storage, amenity fees, application fees, and utility billing.

RUBS

Ratio utility billing system: splitting the building's water, sewer and trash bills among tenants by a formula.

Effective gross incomeEGI

GPR minus vacancy, concessions and bad debt, plus other income.

Trade-out

Rent change on a unit: new lease vs. the prior lease ("new lease trade-out") or renewal vs. expiring rent.

Retention / turnover

Share of tenants who renew. Each move-out costs vacancy days plus turn costs.

Absorption (lease-up pace)

Net new leases per month at a new building, often 15–30 for a mid-size project.

03Expenses

Opex per unit

Annual operating expenses ÷ units, e.g. $6,000–9,000 depending on market, age and taxes.

Expense ratio

Opex ÷ EGI. Typically 35–45%.

Controllable vs. non-controllable

Controllable: payroll, repairs, marketing, turns. Non-controllable: property taxes, insurance, utilities.

Turn cost / make-ready

Paint, cleaning and repairs to re-lease a unit after a move-out.

Management fee

Usually 2.5–4% of EGI for third-party property management.

Replacement reserve

Annual set-aside for roofs, appliances and other capital items, often $250–400 per unit. Lenders require it.

Property tax reassessment

Many jurisdictions reset taxes on sale, so the buyer's taxes can be much higher than the seller's. Always underwrite post-sale taxes.

Tax abatement / PILOT

Reduced property taxes for a period, often in exchange for affordable units (e.g. NYC's 485-x program).

04Value-add & operations

Rent roll

Unit-by-unit list of tenants, rents, lease dates, deposits and balances owed. The first document you review.

T-12 / T-3 annualized

Trailing 12 months of income and expenses; T-3 annualized uses the latest 3 months × 4 to show the current run rate.

Interior renovation

Upgrading units (kitchens, baths, flooring, fixtures, washer/dryer) to charge a rent premium.

Rent premium & renovation ROI

Premium × 12 ÷ renovation cost. $200/month premium on a $15,000 renovation is a 16% return.

Deferred maintenance

Repairs the previous owner skipped. Must be fixed before renovations add value.

Down units

Units that can't be rented until repaired.

Unit mix

Share of studios, 1-, 2- and 3-bedroom units. Drives rent per SF and tenant profile.

Revenue management software

Pricing tools that set daily asking rents by unit. Under legal scrutiny in several places.

05Development

Density (units per acre)

Garden ~20–30, podium ~60–120, high-rise several hundred. Set by zoning.

Building efficiency

Net rentable SF ÷ gross SF, ~80–85% for apartments.

Untrended vs. trended yield on cost

Untrended: stabilized NOI at today's rents ÷ cost. Trended: rents grown to the stabilization date. IC usually wants to see both.

Merchant build

Build, lease up and sell, rather than hold.

Inclusionary zoning

Requirement to set aside a share of units as affordable, sometimes in exchange for extra density or tax breaks.

Lease-up concessions

Free rent offered to fill a new building. Burns off as the building stabilizes.

06Financing

Agency debt

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans for stabilized apartments: long-term, fixed or floating, often the cheapest debt available.

HUD 221(d)(4)

Government-insured construction-to-permanent loan with high leverage and a 40-year term, but slow to close.

Bridge loan

Short-term floating-rate loan for value-add deals, usually with future funding for renovations.

Interest rate cap

Hedge required on floating-rate loans that pays out if rates rise above a strike. Expiring caps caused many 2021-era bridge loan defaults.

DSCR, LTV, debt yield

Agency lenders mainly size to ~1.25x DSCR and ~65–75% LTV.

Negative leverage

When the loan's interest rate is above the cap rate, so debt lowers your cash yield instead of raising it.

07Condos & conversions

Gross sellout

Total sales revenue if every condo unit sells at projected prices.

Sellable SF

Area of the units you can sell, the basis for price per SF.

Presales & deposits

Contracts signed before completion, with 10–20% deposits held in escrow. Construction lenders often require a minimum presale level.

Absorption (sales pace)

Units sold per month. Slower sales mean more interest and carry.

Offering plan

The disclosure document filed with regulators before selling condos. In New York, it's filed with the Attorney General's office.

Release price

Amount of each unit sale that goes to the construction lender to pay down the loan, often 100% until it's repaid.

Inventory loan

Loan secured by unsold finished units, used to pay off the construction loan and give more time to sell.

Margin on cost

Profit ÷ total cost. Condo developers often target 20–25%+ to compensate for sales risk.

Common charges / HOA

Monthly fees owners pay for building operations and the reserve fund.

Condo conversion

Turning an existing rental building into condos. Governed by local tenant protection rules.

Insider price

Discounted price offered to existing tenants in a conversion.

Non-eviction plan

A conversion where existing tenants can stay as renters if they don't buy. Common in New York.

No multifamily terms match that filter.

Plan: a 6-story podium building with 280 units, structured parking, ground-floor amenities and a roof deck.

Case 2 · For-sale development

60-unit boutique condominium

IC memo · illustrative

An infill site in a sought-after urban neighborhood where new condos sell for about $1,600/SF and few are under construction. Plan: a 9-story, 60-unit building with 80,000 gross SF and 60,000 sellable SF (75% efficiency), averaging 1,000 SF and $1.6M per unit.

Step 1How condos differ from rentals

  • You underwrite a sale, not an income stream. Value = units × price. There's no cap rate and no NOI.
  • The risk is sales pace and price. Every month a unit sits unsold costs interest, taxes and common charges.
  • Profit is measured as margin on cost and equity multiple, not yield on cost.
  • Lenders want presales. Signed contracts with large deposits prove demand before or during construction.

Case 3 · Distressed acquisition, value-add & long-term hold

240-unit 1970s garden complex

IC memo · live model

A 1970s Class C garden community in a growing suburb. The prior owner bought it in 2021 with a floating-rate bridge loan. When rates rose and the rate cap expired, they ran out of cash, stopped maintenance and lost control of operations. Occupancy is 78%, delinquency is 10%, and 20 units are down. The lender is selling the loan. Our plan is to fix it and hold it for steady rental income.

Step 1Diagnose before you price

  • Physical: roof leaks, aging HVAC, old galvanized plumbing, 20 down units. Get a full property condition report and walk every unit.
  • Operational: weak screening, high delinquency, slow turns, no RUBS. These are fixable with new management.
  • Market: renovated comparables in the submarket rent for ~$1,700, versus $1,350 in-place. The location is fine.
  • Legal: check local rent control, eviction timelines and code violations on record.

Step 3Business plan & budget

  1. Replace management and clean up the rent roll: collections, evictions where necessary, better screening.
  2. Fix life-safety and deferred maintenance first: roofs, HVAC, plumbing, down units.
  3. Renovate interiors as units turn over: new kitchens, LVP flooring, lighting, fixtures, washer/dryer hookups.
  4. Refresh the exterior and amenities: paint, signage, lighting, cameras, clubhouse, dog park.
  5. Add RUBS, pet rent and covered parking for other income.

Case 4 · Rental-to-condo conversion

80-unit 1960s mid-rise

IC memo · live model

An 80-unit, 8-story elevator building in a walkable urban neighborhood with good schools. All units are market-rate, and most leases expire within 12 months. As a rental it's worth about $345k per unit, but renovated condos nearby sell for about $750/SF, roughly $675k per unit. Plan: buy, renovate and sell the units as condos.

Step 1The arbitrage

As a rentalAs condos

Conversions work when owner-occupiers will pay much more per unit than investors will. That happens in neighborhoods where people want to buy but there's little for-sale supply.

Step 2Is the building suitable?

  • Unit layouts that buyers want: real bedrooms, enough closets, in-unit laundry potential.
  • Building systems that will pass an engineer's report for the offering plan: roof, facade, elevators, boiler, plumbing, electrical.
  • No rent regulation on the units, and local conversion rules that allow it.
  • Mortgage-friendly: buyers' lenders (and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac) have rules on presales, owner occupancy and reserves before they'll lend in a new condo.

Step 3Budget

Line item$MPer unit

Step 4Sellout & profit

$M

What moves the dealProfitMargin on costLevered IRRMultiple

Step 5Process & risks

  1. Buy the building with a bridge loan (60% LTC, $24.5M).
  2. Hire condo counsel and an engineer; prepare and file the offering plan (~6–9 months).
  3. Offer existing tenants an insider price and relocation help; renovate units as they become vacant.
  4. Sell units over ~24 months; each closing pays down the loan until it's repaid.
  • Tenant law: rules vary widely. In New York, a "non-eviction" plan lets tenants who don't buy stay as renters, and since the 2019 rent law changes a majority of tenants in occupancy must agree to buy before such a plan takes effect. That makes conversions of occupied NYC buildings very difficult. Always confirm current rules with counsel.
  • Sales pace and price: the same risks as new condos, with an older building.
  • Hidden building problems found during renovation, and liability to buyers for defects afterward.
  • Unsold units: the sponsor keeps paying common charges and may rent them out, leaving a partly sold building.

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer.

Q1A 200-unit building has 95% physical occupancy but 88% economic occupancy. What explains the gap?

Show answer

Rent that's owed or potential but not collected: concessions, bad debt, loss-to-lease (in-place rents below market) and non-revenue units like a model or staff unit. Check the rent roll and the delinquency report to see which.

Q2A $15,000 renovation earns a $175/month premium. At a 5.5% cap, is it worth it?

Show answer

$175 × 12 = $2,100 a year, a 14% return on cost. Value created is $2,100 ÷ 5.5% ≈ $38,000 per unit, more than double the $15,000 spent. Yes, assuming the premium is real and turnover doesn't rise.

Q3Why might a 1-bedroom earn more per SF than a 3-bedroom in the same building?

Show answer

Kitchens and bathrooms are the expensive parts, and every unit needs one. Renters pay for having a home, not just for square feet, so smaller units command higher rent per SF while larger units command more rent in total.

Q4When would you build condos instead of rentals on the same site?

Show answer

When sale prices per SF are high enough that the condo margin beats the rental development spread, and buyer demand is deep. Rentals are better when cap rates are low relative to construction costs, when you want long-term income, or when condo sales are risky (thin buyer pool, tough mortgage environment).

Q5The previous owner of Case 3 had a floating-rate bridge loan. What went wrong, and how does the new plan avoid it?

Show answer

Rates rose, the rate cap expired and buying a new one was expensive, so interest costs jumped while the business plan was unfinished. The new plan uses a cap during the turnaround, keeps more cushion for shortfalls, and refinances into fixed-rate agency debt once the property is stable.

Multifamily · Affordable housing

Affordable Housing

The same apartment buildings, financed a different way. Rents are capped by tenant income, so deals rely on tax credits, tax-exempt bonds and public loans to cover what rents alone can't support.

Max rent = 30% of the income limit for the unit's assumed household size (1.5 people per bedroom), minus a utility allowance. The rent you actually get is the lower of that and market rent.

01Income & rent limits

Area median incomeAMI

The middle household income in a metro area, published by HUD each year by household size. Every affordable rent and income limit is a percentage of it.

Income bands

Extremely low (≤30% AMI), very low (≤50%), low (≤80%), moderate (80–120%+). Programs target specific bands.

Income limit

The most a household can earn to qualify for a unit, e.g. 60% of AMI for its size.

Rent limit

Usually 30% of the income limit, divided by 12. Based on an assumed household size, not who actually lives there.

Imputed household size

For LIHTC rent limits: 1 person for a studio, 1.5 people per bedroom otherwise.

Utility allowanceUA

Estimated tenant-paid utilities, subtracted from the gross rent limit to get the maximum rent the owner can charge.

Gross vs. net rent

Gross: rent limit including utilities. Net: what the owner collects after the utility allowance.

Hold harmless

LIHTC rule that generally keeps a project's rent limits from falling when HUD's published AMI drops.

Rent burden

Rent as a share of household income. Over 30% is "cost-burdened," over 50% "severely."

02LIHTC basics

LIHTC

Low-Income Housing Tax Credit: a federal tax credit given to owners of qualifying rental housing over 10 years. Developers sell the credits to investors for equity.

9% credits

Larger credits (about 70% of eligible costs in present value) awarded competitively by each state. Limited and very competitive.

4% credits

Smaller credits (about 30% in present value) that come automatically when a project is financed with enough tax-exempt bonds. Most large deals use these.

Qualified Allocation PlanQAP

Each state's rules and scoring for awarding credits: location, affordability depth, cost limits, services.

Eligible basis

Depreciable development costs: building and most soft costs. Excludes land, and often some financing and reserve costs.

Basis boost

Eligible basis can be increased up to 130% in high-cost or low-income areas (QCTs and DDAs), raising the credits.

Applicable fraction

Share of the building that's affordable (lower of the unit share and the floor-area share). 100% for fully affordable buildings.

Qualified basis

Eligible basis × boost × applicable fraction. Credits = qualified basis × credit rate, each year for 10 years.

Minimum set-aside

The election that defines the project's affordability: 20% of units at 50% AMI, 40% at 60% AMI, or income averaging.

Income averaging

Units can serve bands from 20% to 80% AMI as long as the average is 60% or less. Lets a project mix deeper and shallower affordability.

Compliance period & extended use

15 years of federal compliance, plus extended affordability (typically 30+ years total, often longer under state or city rules).

Recapture

Investors can lose credits already taken if the project falls out of compliance during the compliance period.

Form 8609

IRS form issued after completion that confirms the credits. Final equity payments usually wait for it.

03Capital stack & players

Sources & uses

Affordable deals are underwritten by making sources (loans, equity, subsidies) equal total development cost. The shortfall is the "gap."

Tax credit investor

Usually a bank or large corporation buying credits to reduce taxes. Banks also earn Community Reinvestment Act credit.

Syndicator

Firm that pools investors into funds, buys credits from developers and manages compliance.

Credit pricing

Dollars of equity per dollar of credit, e.g. $0.88. Falls when investor demand or tax rates fall, or when rates rise.

Equity pay-ins

Tax credit equity arrives in installments: some at closing, more at completion, the rest after stabilization and Form 8609.

Private activity bonds & volume cap

Tax-exempt bonds that finance 4% deals. Each state has a limited annual allotment ("volume cap").

50% / 25% bond test

To earn 4% credits, tax-exempt bonds must finance at least 50% of land plus building basis. A 2025 federal law lowered this to 25% for bonds issued after 2025, stretching scarce bond cap across more deals.

Soft / gap financing

Low-interest public loans (city, state, HOME funds) that fill the gap. Usually repaid only from leftover cash flow ("residual receipts").

Deferred developer fee

Part of the developer's fee left unpaid and repaid from future cash flow, acting as a source of funds.

Housing finance agencyHFA

State or city agency that allocates credits and bonds and often lends. In NYC: HPD and HDC.

Community Reinvestment ActCRA

Federal law encouraging banks to invest in their communities. A major reason banks buy tax credits and make affordable loans.

04Rental assistance

Housing Choice Voucher

Tenant-based Section 8: the tenant pays ~30% of income and the housing authority pays the rest to the landlord, up to a payment standard.

Project-based Section 8

Rental assistance attached to specific units through a HUD contract, so it stays with the building, not the tenant.

HAP contract

Housing Assistance Payments contract setting the "contract rent" HUD pays on project-based units. Renewals typically run 1–20 years.

Payment standard

The maximum rent a voucher will cover in an area, set by the housing authority.

Rent reasonableness

Voucher rents can't exceed rents for comparable unassisted units nearby.

Mark-to-Market / Mark-up-to-Market

HUD programs that reset project-based contract rents down to market (if above) or up to market (if below) at renewal.

RAD

Rental Assistance Demonstration: converts public housing to project-based Section 8 so owners can borrow and use tax credits for repairs.

05Operations, compliance & NYC programs

Tenant income certification

Verifying each household's income at move-in (and often yearly) to prove the unit qualifies.

Regulatory agreement

Recorded document that binds the property to its income and rent limits for the affordability period.

Year 15

End of the federal compliance period. The investor typically exits, and the developer or a nonprofit buys out its interest, often resyndicating with new credits.

Operating & replacement reserves

Cash cushions lenders and investors require at closing, often 6 months of expenses plus annual replacement deposits.

HPD / HDC

NYC's housing preservation department and housing development corporation: the city's main sources of subsidy loans and bonds.

485-x

NYC property tax exemption for new rental buildings that include affordable units, replacing 421-a. Requirements vary by project size.

Mandatory Inclusionary HousingMIH

NYC zoning that requires a share of permanently affordable units when an area is rezoned for more density.

Housing lottery

How NYC affordable units are leased: applications through the city's Housing Connect portal, then random selection and income checks.

No affordable housing terms match that filter.

Topic 1How interest rates affect affordable deal flow

Affordable rents are capped by income, not by the market, so owners can't raise rents to cover higher interest costs. When rates rise, the project can carry less debt, and the difference has to come from somewhere else.

Interest rates rise
Permanent loan
Same capped NOI supports a smaller loan at the same DSCR
Construction
Construction and bond interest cost more, raising total cost
Equity
Investors want higher yields, so tax credit pricing can fall
Gap widensMore public subsidy needed per unit
Is enough subsidy available?
Yes
Deal closes, but subsidy covers fewer units in total
No
Deal is delayed, redesigned or dropped

Example using Case 1 (200 units, $2.59M NOI, loan sized at 1.20x DSCR on a 40-year amortization):

Perm rate 6.25%Perm rate 7.25%Change
Permanent loan$31.6M$28.1M–$3.6M
Tax credit price$0.88$0.85–$1.4M equity
Construction & bond interestbasehigher~+$1.5M cost
Added gap~$6.5M (~$32k/unit)
  • Credit rates no longer move with interest rates. The 9% and 4% rates are now fixed minimums in federal law, so higher rates don't reduce the credit amount itself.
  • Subsidy becomes the bottleneck. City and state budgets are fixed, so a bigger gap per deal means fewer deals per year.
  • Bond cap matters more. The lower 25% bond test (for bonds issued after 2025) lets the same volume cap support more projects, partly offsetting tighter conditions.
  • Lower rates work in reverse: bigger loans, smaller gaps and more deals.

Topic 2When the affordable rent limit is above market rent

Rent limits are calculated from area-wide incomes. In a weaker neighborhood, the legal maximum for a 60% or 80% AMI unit can be higher than what renters there actually pay. The limit is a ceiling, not a guarantee.

Example: 2 BR in a weaker submarketMonthly
80% AMI rent limit (net of utilities)$2,820
Market rent for a comparable unit$2,300
Rent you can actually charge$2,300
  • You charge the lower of the two. Tenants won't pay more than the market just because the law allows it. Underwrite achievable rent, not the limit.
  • Smaller loan and more gap. Lenders size on achievable rents, so the project borrows less than the rent schedule implied.
  • Income averaging can break. Deals that offset deep 30% AMI units with 70–80% AMI units rely on those higher rents. If the market can't support them, the average still works for compliance but the income doesn't.
  • Leasing gets harder at higher bands. A household earning 80% of AMI may have market options nearby at the same rent and fewer restrictions.
  • Vouchers don't fix it. Rent reasonableness caps voucher-paid rents at comparable market rents.
  • Project-based Section 8: HUD's Mark-to-Market process can cut contract rents that are above market at renewal, which can leave the property unable to support its existing debt and force a restructuring.
  • It's a signal. If limits exceed market rents, the affordable units may not be serving anyone the market wasn't already serving. Agencies may push for deeper affordability (lower bands) in those locations.

Try it in the LIHTC rent calculator on the Terminology tab: set market rent below the max net rent and watch the achievable rent and the read change.

Case 2 · Acquisition-rehab preservation

150-unit Section 8 building at Year 15

IC memo · illustrative

A 1980s, 150-unit building with a project-based Section 8 contract on every unit. Its original tax credit compliance period has ended, the building needs about $80,000 per unit of work, and the HAP contract is up for renewal. The old partnership wants to sell. Plan: buy it, renew the HAP contract for 20 years, rehab with new 4% credits and keep it affordable for another 30+ years.

Step 1Why this is a good deal

  • Guaranteed rent. HUD pays most of the rent under the HAP contract, so income is very stable.
  • Rents can go up. The current contract rent is below market, so at renewal HUD's Mark-up-to-Market process can raise it.
  • Credits on the purchase. Buying an existing building qualifies for 4% "acquisition credits" on the building's value, on top of rehab credits.
  • Mission. Without new investment, the building could deteriorate or leave the affordable stock.

Because the HAP contract makes the rent so reliable, the permanent loan covers more of the cost than in Case 1, and no new city subsidy is needed.

Step 4Process & risks

  1. Negotiate purchase with the old partnership; obtain HUD consent to transfer the HAP contract.
  2. Request a 20-year HAP renewal with a rent comparability study supporting a mark-up.
  3. Apply for bonds and 4% credits; close financing.
  4. Rehab with tenants in place (unit by unit, a few days each), with temporary relocation where needed.
  • Federal appropriations: HAP payments depend on Congress funding HUD each year.
  • Tenant-in-place rehab is slower and costlier than vacant rehab.
  • Rent study risk: if the comparability study comes in low, rents and the loan shrink.
  • Hidden conditions in a 40-year-old building.
Credit lensLenders like Section 8-backed loans for their stable income, often through FHA-insured or agency affordable programs. The key diligence is the HAP contract term, renewal terms and whether contract rents could be reset down to market later.

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer.

Q1Why can't an affordable deal just raise rents when interest rates go up?

Show answer

Rents are capped by AMI-based limits written into the regulatory agreement. Higher rates shrink the loan the same NOI can support, so the gap must be filled with more subsidy, a deferred fee or a lower cost.

Q2What's the difference between 9% and 4% credits?

Show answer

9% credits are larger (about 70% of eligible costs in present value) but awarded competitively by the state. 4% credits are smaller (about 30%) but come automatically when tax-exempt bonds finance enough of the project, so they're used for most large deals.

Q3A 2BR 80% AMI rent limit is $2,820 but nearby market rent is $2,300. What do you underwrite?

Show answer

$2,300 or a bit less: the achievable rent, not the legal maximum. Expect a smaller loan, possibly slower leasing at that band, and check whether income averaging still produces enough revenue.

Q4Why do banks buy tax credits at $0.85–0.95 when they're worth $1 of tax savings?

Show answer

The credits arrive over 10 years and carry compliance and recapture risk, so investors pay a discount that produces a reasonable after-tax yield. Banks also earn Community Reinvestment Act credit, which can push prices higher.

Q5In Case 3, why does setting aside 75 affordable units increase the building's value?

Show answer

The property tax exemption it unlocks (~$3.8M a year) is much larger than the rent given up on the affordable units (~$1.3M a year), so NOI rises by over $2.5M even after the higher cost.

Core concept · Capital markets

Capital Stack

Every dollar of a deal comes from someone, and each of those people holds a different claim. The stack ranks those claims: who gets paid first, who loses first, and what each layer charges for where it sits.

Two orders, opposite directions

Payment priority runs top-down: senior first, common last

Loss absorption runs bottom-up: common first, senior last

Cost of capital rises as you move toward the first loss

All three cases here are ground-up developments with a construction-loan stack, run through a live waterfall.

Module 01

The stack, layer by layer

Start with a stabilized $100M apartment building. Every module comes back to this picture. The question for each layer is where its claim attaches (the first dollar of value it's exposed to) and where it detaches.

Common equity85–100% · $15M
Preferred equity75–85% · $10M
Mezzanine loan60–75% · $15M
Senior mortgage0–60% · $60M
LayerSecured byReturn formTypical cost
Senior mortgageMortgage on the real propertyContract interest6–7%
Mezzanine loanPledge of the borrower's LLC interestsContract interest (+ fees)10–13%
Preferred equityEquity in the owner entity, with control rightsFixed preferred return, sometimes a kicker11–15%
Common equityResidual ownershipWhatever's left, split by the waterfall15%+ target

Loss slider: who gets hurt?

Drag the value down. Losses eat the stack from the bottom up, and each layer is safe until the loss reaches its attachment point.

Read it like a lender: "We're in at 60 to 75. A 25% value decline doesn't touch us; at 30% we lose a third of our money; at 40% we're wiped out."

VocabularyTerms you'll hear on every deal

Attachment / detachment

The value range a layer is exposed to. Mezz "60–75" means it loses nothing until value falls below 75% of today's level.

Last-dollar LTV

The detachment point as a percentage of value. A mezz lender at 75% last-dollar has 25% equity cushion beneath it.

Basis

Value at which your money is exposed. "Lending at a $180k/unit basis" in a market where replacement cost is $300k/unit is a strong position.

Sources & uses

Uses (land, hard costs, soft costs, financing, fees) must equal sources (each layer). Every case below starts here.

Module 02

Senior debt: permanent vs. construction

Who lendsSenior lender types

LenderSweet spotTypical terms
BanksConstruction, transitional, relationship lendingFloating, 50–65% LTC, partial or full recourse
Agency (Fannie / Freddie)Stabilized multifamilyFixed, up to ~75–80% LTV, non-recourse
CMBS conduitStabilized commercial assets10-yr fixed, often IO, non-recourse, defeasance
Life companiesLow-leverage, high-quality assetsLong fixed-rate, 50–60% LTV, lowest spreads
Debt fundsBridge, transitional, constructionFloating, higher leverage, higher spread

Loan sizing: the lowest of three tests

Permanent lenders size to whichever constraint binds first: LTV, DSCR or debt yield.

LTV test
—
DSCR test
—
Debt yield test
—
Max loan
—
Binding
—

Construction loansHow they differ from permanent loans

Sized on cost, not value

Loan-to-cost (LTC) is typically 50–65% of total development cost (TDC). There's no NOI yet, so lenders also check projected yield on cost and a stress LTV on the as-stabilized value.

Equity goes in first

The lender funds nothing until the full equity requirement, and any mezz or pref, has been spent. After that, the loan funds monthly draws against inspected work, less retainage (5–10% held until completion).

Interest is budgeted

An interest reserve inside the budget pays interest until the property produces cash, so construction interest is part of TDC. Run out of reserve and the sponsor pays.

The sponsor guarantees

Completion guarantee (finish the building), carry guarantee (interest, taxes, insurance until stabilization), and often partial repayment recourse (25–50%) that burns off at stabilization.

CloseEquity funds

Land, design, early hard costs

BuildLoan draws

Monthly, inspected, retainage held

Lease-upInterest reserve

Carries debt until NOI arrives

StabilizeTakeout

Refi with a perm loan, or sell

Takeout riskA construction loan is repaid by someone else's money: the permanent lender or a buyer. If rates rise or the cap rate widens during the 2–3 year build, the perm loan may be smaller than the construction loan. That shortfall is a refinance gap, and the sponsor has to fill it with new equity, rescue pref, or an extension. Most construction-era distress in 2023–25 was exactly this.

TermsWhat else is in a senior loan

  • Rate: fixed vs. floating (SOFR + spread). Floating-rate loans usually require an interest rate cap.
  • Prepayment: yield maintenance or defeasance (fixed rate), or open after a lockout (floating).
  • Recourse: full, partial or non-recourse. "Non-recourse" loans still carry bad-boy carve-outs (fraud, voluntary bankruptcy, unpermitted transfers) that make the guarantor liable.
  • Cash management: springing lockbox and cash sweep if DSCR or debt yield falls below a trigger.
  • Extension options: for floating-rate loans, usually 1-year extensions conditioned on DSCR or debt-yield tests and a new rate cap.

Module 03

The middle of the stack

Between the senior loan and the sponsor's equity sit layers that fill the gap. Each is designed around one question: how fast can I take control if things go wrong?

B-note (A/B structure)

One mortgage split into a senior A-note and a junior B-note. Both are secured by the same real property. A co-lender agreement sets the payment priority and gives the B-note holder control rights until its position is "appraised out."

Mezzanine loan

A loan to the parent of the property owner, secured by a pledge of the LLC interests, not by the property. On default, the mezz lender forecloses through a UCC sale in roughly 30–60 days and steps into ownership, still subject to the senior loan. A judicial mortgage foreclosure can take 1–3 years.

Intercreditor agreementWhere the real negotiation happens

  • Cure rights: mezz may cure senior defaults to stop a foreclosure.
  • Purchase option: mezz may buy the senior loan at par once it's in default.
  • Qualified transferee: who can own the property after a mezz foreclosure (net worth and experience tests, replacement guarantor).
  • Standstill / consent rights: what each lender can do without the other, e.g. modifications, extensions, releases.

Preferred equityDebt economics, equity form

Hard pref

A fixed return (often 11–15%), a mandatory redemption date, and strong remedies: removing the sponsor, forcing a sale, taking over management. Behaves like debt.

Soft pref

Paid from available cash flow, with no fixed maturity and weaker remedies. Behaves more like equity: priority, but no hammer.

Why use pref instead of mezz? Many senior lenders (agency especially) prohibit mezz debt but allow pref equity, because it isn't technically debt. Pref also doesn't count toward the borrower's debt for loan covenants.

Credit lensMezz and pref are where much of the yield in CRE credit lives. Underwrite them with three questions. What's our basis (last-dollar LTV vs. replacement cost)? How fast can we take control? Would we be happy to own the asset at our basis?

Module 04

Waterfall mechanics

The waterfall is how the common equity splits what's left after the debt and pref are paid. The investor (LP) supplies most of the capital; the sponsor (GP) finds, builds and runs the deal. The waterfall pays the GP a promote (a disproportionate share of profit) only once the LP has earned a set return.

Tier 1Return of capital + preferred return

100% pro rata (LP 90 / GP 10) until LP has an 8% IRR on its money.

Tier 2 (optional)GP catch-up

A larger share (50–100%) to the GP until it has received its target share of all profit so far.

Tier 3First promote

80 / 20 (20% promote to GP) until LP reaches the next IRR hurdle, e.g. 13%.

Tier 4+Higher promotes

70 / 30, then 60 / 40 as LP returns clear each hurdle.

The building blocksEach one changes who gets paid

TermWhat it meansWho it favors
Preferred returnLP's minimum return before any promote. Usually 7–10%. Cumulative means any shortfall carries forward.LP
Compounding vs. simpleAn IRR-based pref compounds. A simple pref accrues on contributed capital only. Compounding favors LP on long or delayed deals.LP (compounding)
Return of capital firstLP gets all money back before any promote. Standard in development deals.LP
Catch-upAfter the pref, GP receives a large share until it has its full promote percentage of total profit. With a 100% catch-up and 20% promote, the pref effectively becomes a threshold, not a floor.GP
IRR hurdlesPromote steps up at each LP IRR level. Rewards speed: a quick sale clears hurdles easily.GP on fast deals
Equity multiple hurdlesHurdles stated as 1.5x or 2.0x, sometimes combined with IRR ("greater of"). Stops a GP being promoted on a tiny-dollar, high-IRR flip.LP
Deal-by-deal (American)Promote calculated and paid per deal. A loser in deal 3 doesn't claw back promote from deal 1.GP
Whole-fund (European)No promote until LPs get back all fund capital plus pref. Standard in closed-end funds.LP
ClawbackIf early promote turns out to be excessive once the fund finishes, the GP returns it (often net of taxes, backed by a guarantee).LP
GP co-investThe sponsor's own money, typically 5–10%. It earns pro rata returns plus the promote.Alignment
FeesAcquisition, development (inside TDC), asset management, disposition. Paid regardless of performance, which is why LPs watch them.GP

Not the same thingMultiple hurdles vs. double promote

Multiple IRR hurdles (Case B)

One sponsor, one waterfall. The GP's share steps up from 20% to 30% to 40% as the LP's IRR clears 13%, then 17%. The LP pays one promote, at a rate that rises with performance.

Double promote (Case C)

Two sponsors in a chain. A local developer earns a promote at the deal level. The fund that invested earns its own carried interest from its investors on what's left. The end investor pays two promotes: one inside the deal, one at the fund.

Module 05 · Case A

Single pref + promote: 240-unit garden apartments

A local developer (GP) builds 240 garden-style units in a growing Sun Belt suburb with one institutional LP. It's the simplest common-equity waterfall: 8% pref, then 80 / 20. Build for 3 years, refinance at stabilization, sell at the end of Year 6.

Construction loan $36M60% LTC · SOFR + 3.25% · 3 yrs + 2×1

The takeout: stabilized NOI at a 5.25% refinance cap gives a value of about $74M. An agency loan at 65% LTV (5.75%, interest-only) is about $48M. That repays the $36M construction loan and returns roughly $12M to equity at Year 3. A cost overrun is funded by equity, which raises the equity check.

Run the waterfall

Tiers: (1) 100% pro rata until LP has an 8% IRR; (2) 80% pro rata / 20% promote to GP thereafter.

Read the resultAt the base case the deal returns ~1.8x and ~13.6%. The LP nets less than the deal (~12.6%) because the GP takes 20% of everything above 8%. The GP's own IRR is far higher than the deal's: its 10% co-invest earns pro rata returns plus the promote. Try a 6% exit cap with a 5% overrun: the promote disappears and both sides earn the same low return. That's the alignment the pref is supposed to create.

A merchant build: develop a Class A distribution building, lease it up and sell at the end of Year 3. The stack adds a mezz loan, and the equity waterfall has a catch-up and three promote tiers. That's the typical shape for an institutional programmatic JV.

025.025.0——

3Lease-up, then sale at year end: price − 1.5% costs − $55M senior − $10M mezz = equity proceeds

Run the waterfall

(1) Pro rata to 8% LP IRR → (2) 50% catch-up until GP promote = 20% of profit → (3) 80 / 20 to 13% → (4) 70 / 30 to 17% → (5) 60 / 40 thereafter.

What to noticeWhy each feature exists

  • The catch-up: once the LP has its 8%, half of each dollar goes to the GP as promote until the GP holds 20% of all profit. After that, the deal looks as if the GP took 20% from the first dollar of profit. Without a catch-up, the GP's 20% applies only to profit above the pref.
  • Rising tiers reward outperformance. At a 5.25% exit cap the deal reaches the 60 / 40 tier and the GP's promote roughly doubles. At 6.25% with an overrun, nothing clears the 8% pref.
  • The mezz changes the equity math. Leverage rises from 55% to 65% of cost. That boosts equity IRR in the upside, and the equity is wiped out sooner in the downside (see Module 08).
  • Merchant build = IRR-friendly. A three-year hold clears IRR hurdles with less total profit than a long hold would. That's why LPs often add an equity-multiple test (e.g. promote only above 1.5x).

Module 07 · Case C

Double promote: 300-unit high-rise with pref equity

A value-add fund partners with a local operating partner (OP) to build a high-rise. The construction lender caps senior debt at 55% LTC, so a third party fills the gap with hard preferred equity. The common equity then runs through two waterfalls: the deal-level JV (OP promote) and the fund's own carry to its investors.

Construction stack

Common $45MFund 90 / OP 10 · first in
Pref $22.5M55–70% · 12% compounding
Senior $82.5M0–55% LTC · ~7%

Hard pref: accrues 12% compounding with mandatory redemption at sale or refinance. It can remove the OP and force a sale on default.

Deal levelProject cash → senior → pref → common
JV waterfallCommon split: Fund 90 / OP 10

9% pref → 80 / 20 to 15% IRR → 70 / 30 thereafter. Promote #1 to the OP.

Fund waterfallFund's share → fund investors

Run both waterfalls

Build Years 0–2, lease-up Year 3, sell at the end of Year 4. Pref is repaid in full before common receives anything.

The cost of two promotesThe common equity earns its deal-level return. The fund keeps less after the OP's promote, and its investors keep less again after the fund manager's carry. Each layer can be fair on its own, but the end investor pays both. That's why LPs negotiate fee and promote offsets, or invest directly in the JV ("co-invest") to skip the second layer.

Module 08

Stress & workouts

Leverage magnifies both directions. The same building can make the equity a hero or wipe it out, while the senior lender barely notices.

Leverage: positive or negative?

If the property's unlevered return is below the cost of debt, adding leverage lowers equity returns.

Levered return
—
Leverage effect
—
Formula
Levered = U + (U − K) × D/E. Each turn of debt-to-equity adds the spread (U − K), positive or negative.

WorkoutsWhat each seat can do

Senior lender

Extend and modify ("amend and extend"), take a cash sweep, require a paydown, sell the note, appoint a receiver, or foreclose. Recovery depends on basis and on whether the market is liquid.

Mezz lender

Cure senior defaults to protect its position, buy the senior loan at par, or UCC-foreclose on the equity and take over the property, subject to the senior loan. It must decide quickly whether its position is in the money.

Pref equity

Remove the sponsor, take over management, force a sale. Its accrued return keeps compounding while it waits.

Common equity

Inject rescue capital (usually new senior-to-common pref), negotiate a discounted payoff, hand back the keys (deed-in-lieu), or hold on and hope. A recap that dilutes old equity is often the best outcome.

PatternThe refinance gap, in numbers

Take Case A. The $36M construction loan was sized when the stabilized value was projected at ~$74M (3.9M NOI at a 5.25% cap). Suppose that by Year 3 lease-up comes in 10% light (NOI $3.5M) and the market cap rate is 6.5%. Value is now ~$54M, a 65% LTV perm loan is ~$35M, and a 1.25x DSCR at 7% on 30-year amortization also gives ~$35M. The sponsor is $1–2M short of repaying the construction loan after closing costs, with no cash-out at all. Options: extend (if the tests are met), bring new equity, raise rescue pref, or sell. This is the distressed-credit opportunity set.

Module 09

Special layers & the credit lens

Ground lease

Sits below the senior loan. An unsubordinated ground rent is paid before debt service. It lowers the cost of the land, but it caps how much the leasehold can borrow.

C-PACE

Financing for energy and resiliency work, repaid through a property tax assessment. Because tax liens are senior, C-PACE can rank ahead of the mortgage. Most senior lenders require consent.

Public capital

LIHTC equity, tax-exempt bonds, TIF and soft loans fill affordable housing stacks (see the Affordable Housing tab). They often have long-dated or cash-flow-only payment terms.

Seller financing & earn-outs

A seller note or deferred payment sits between the debt and equity. It's often subordinate, sometimes contingent on performance.

Credit lensHow a lender or credit investor reads any stack

  1. Where do we attach and detach? Last-dollar LTV, and basis per unit or SF against replacement cost and recent sales.
  2. What's below us? Real cash equity vs. "equity" from fees, land write-ups, or pref that's really debt.
  3. Who's the sponsor and what's guaranteed? Track record, net worth and liquidity, completion and carry guarantees.
  4. How do we get repaid? Takeout loan, sale, or cash flow. What happens if that source shrinks?
  5. How fast can we take control? Mortgage foreclosure vs. UCC, intercreditor rights, state foreclosure timelines.
  6. Would we own it at our basis? If the answer is no, the yield doesn't matter.
Connect itA CMBS B-piece buyer and a mezz lender answer the same questions from different seats: both hold the first-loss position below a large senior claim. The CMBS tab's loss slider is the same idea as Module 01 here, applied to a pool of loans instead of one building.

Module 10

Self-check

Q1A $100M stabilized building has a 60% senior loan and 15% mezz. Value falls 30%. Who takes losses, and how much?

Reveal

Value is $70M. Senior ($60M) is fully covered. Mezz attaches at $60M and detaches at $75M, so it recovers $10M of $15M (a $5M loss). Common equity and any pref below the mezz are wiped out.

Q2Why does a construction lender insist that all equity goes in first?

Reveal

So the sponsor's money absorbs early cost overruns and the lender's exposure always sits on top of real, already-spent equity. If the lender funded alongside equity, a project abandoned halfway could leave it with a half-built asset and very little cushion.

Q3Same deal, two waterfalls: (a) 8% pref then 80 / 20, with no catch-up; (b) 8% pref, 100% catch-up to 20%, then 80 / 20. The deal earns a 15% IRR. Which does the GP prefer, and why?

Reveal

(b). With a catch-up, once the pref is cleared the GP receives 20% of all profit, including the profit that made up the 8%. Without one, the GP gets 20% only of profit above the pref. The gap closes once returns are well above the pref.

Q4An agency lender won't allow mezz on a multifamily refinance. The sponsor needs another 10% of capital. What's the usual answer, and what does the agency lender still care about?

Reveal

Preferred equity. The agency lender will still review its terms, because pref with a hard maturity and control rights behaves like debt and can trigger a change of control. Expect limits on mandatory redemption and on removing the sponsor.

Q5In Case C, why does the fund's investor net IRR fall further below the common equity IRR than the fund's gross IRR does?

Reveal

Two promotes. The OP's promote reduces what the fund receives from the deal (gross). The fund manager's carry, with a full catch-up, then takes another 20% of the fund's profit before its investors are paid (net). Fees would widen the gap further.

Q6Unlevered return 6.5%, debt at 7.25%, 65% LTV. What does leverage do to equity returns?

Reveal

Negative leverage: 6.5% + (6.5% − 7.25%) × 65/35 ≈ 5.1%. Borrowing lowers the equity return. That was common in 2023–24 and is why buyers paid low cap rates only when they underwrote strong rent growth.

NoteAll figures are illustrative and rounded, built on annual periods to show the mechanics. Real models run monthly and include fees, taxes and detailed draw schedules.

Core concept · Credit

Distressed Debt & Special Servicing

When a loan can't be repaid as written, foreclosure is the last resort, not the default answer. Most distressed loans end in a negotiated outcome. The job is to find the resolution worth the most today to whoever owns the loan, and to get the borrower to agree to it.

The servicer's test (CMBS)

Pick the option with the highest net present value of recovery for the trust as a whole

Not the option that punishes the borrower, or the one that's fastest

Every conversation in a workout is really an argument about which option has the highest NPV, and who should bear the shortfall.

Module 01

How loans go bad

Distress has two common shapes. A term default: the property can't cover debt service. A maturity default: the property may be paying fine, but the loan can't be refinanced or repaid when it comes due. Since 2023, most CRE distress has been the second kind.

Term (monetary) default

NOI falls below debt service: a tenant leaves, occupancy drops, expenses or a floating rate spike. Missed payments start the clock. In CMBS, a loan 60 days delinquent typically transfers to special servicing.

Maturity default

The loan comes due and no new lender will lend enough to repay it, because rates are higher, values lower, or underwriting tighter. The building may still cover its interest. The problem is the refinance gap.

TriggersWhat sends a loan to workout or special servicing

TriggerExample
Payment default60+ days delinquent on a CMBS loan; 90+ days typically makes a bank loan "non-accrual"
Maturity defaultBalloon not repaid at maturity (or expected not to be)
Imminent defaultThe borrower says it can't pay, or the servicer judges default "reasonably foreseeable" (the standard that lets a CMBS loan be modified at all)
Bankruptcy / insolvencyBorrower or a key tenant files
Material non-monetary defaultUnpermitted transfer, lapsed insurance, unpaid taxes, mechanic's liens

CMBS loans held in REMIC trusts can only be significantly modified when default has occurred or is reasonably foreseeable (Rev. Proc. 2009-45 broadened this). That's why borrowers often must "be in trouble" before the servicer is even allowed to negotiate.

Early warningThe signals before the call

  • Debt yield sliding toward the cash-sweep trigger; DSCR under 1.10x
  • Large tenant notice, dark store, or bankruptcy filing
  • Rate cap expiring; interest reserve running down; extension tests failing
  • Borrower asks "informally" about extension options 6–12 months before maturity
  • Late tax payments, deferred maintenance, sponsor defaults on other loans

Module 02

Who's at the table

Borrower / sponsor

Wants time and to keep its equity option alive. Its leverage: it runs the property, knows the tenants, can put in new money, and can make enforcement slow or expensive.

Guarantor

The sponsor principal who signed the carve-out or other guaranties. Personal exposure is often the biggest single driver of borrower behavior.

Master servicer (CMBS)

Collects payments and advances principal and interest to bondholders. Transfers the loan to the special servicer on a trigger.

Special servicer (CMBS)

Runs the workout for the trust: negotiates, orders appraisals, modifies, forecloses, sells REO. Rialto, LNR, KeyBank, CWCapital, Midland, Trimont and others.

Controlling class / directing holder

Usually the B-piece buyer (the most junior bondholder). It has consent or consultation rights over major decisions while its position is still "in the money."

Operating advisor

Independent monitor in post-2010 CMBS. Reviews special-servicer decisions and conflicts, especially when the servicer is affiliated with the B-piece buyer.

Bank workout group

For balance-sheet loans, a separate team takes over from the relationship lender. It's less constrained than CMBS, but watched by regulators and capital rules.

Others

Mezz lender (cure and purchase rights), receiver, counsel on both sides, appraisers, brokers, and sometimes a rescue capital provider.

Servicer economicsTypical CMBS special servicer fees: a special servicing fee (~0.25% a year on the loan balance), a workout fee (~1% of collections on a modified loan that returns to performing), and a liquidation fee (~1% of proceeds from a DPO, note sale or REO sale). Fee caps and the operating advisor exist because these incentives aren't neutral.

Module 03

The first 90 days after transfer

Day 0Transfer & welcome letter

The special servicer introduces itself, names the asset manager, and sends a reservation of rights letter: defaults exist, nothing said now waives the lender's remedies.

Week 1–2Pre-negotiation letter (PNL)

Both sides sign before talking substance. Discussions are non-binding; there are no oral agreements; nothing waives the default; only a signed modification counts. The borrower often confirms the debt amount. No PNL, no conversation.

Week 1–4Information request

Rent roll, T-12, budget, leasing pipeline and LOIs, capex needs, sponsor financials, the borrower's proposal and business plan, bank statements.

Week 1–4Cash control

Hard lockbox activated or cash sweep enforced. Excess cash is trapped. The servicer may approve a budget so the property keeps running.

Week 3–8Valuation

New appraisal, site inspection, broker opinions of value. In CMBS, the appraisal can create an Appraisal Reduction Amount (ARA) that cuts interest advances to the bottom bonds.

Week 6–12Asset business plan & NPV

The servicer models every option (Module 06), recommends a strategy, and consults or seeks consent from the controlling class.

Month 3–9Negotiate, document, close

Term sheet for the modification (or DPO or deed-in-lieu), documents, approvals, closing. In parallel, the servicer often files foreclosure or seeks a receiver to keep pressure on.

Dual trackingServicers often negotiate and start enforcement (notice of default, foreclosure filing, receiver motion) at the same time. The clock on enforcement is the servicer's leverage, and it keeps the borrower from using the talks just to buy time.

Module 04

The conversation: how a workout actually goes

A composite, condensed negotiation over a $85M CMBS loan on a 410,000 SF suburban office building (the Parkway case in Module 07). The loan matures in six months. Occupancy fell from 91% to 64% when the largest tenant left. Notes on the right explain what each side is really doing.

Round 1 · Six months before maturity

BorrowerWe wanted to get ahead of this. With the lease-up where it is, we can't refinance $85M by July. We're asking for a three-year extension at the current rate. The property still covers its interest, and we've got two LOIs for 60,000 feet.
Calling early is smart. It builds credibility and starts the talks while the borrower still has a performing loan. Leading with "we cover interest" frames this as a timing problem, not a value problem.
ServicerWe appreciate the early call. Before we discuss terms, we'll need a pre-negotiation letter signed, then the rent roll, T-12, leasing pipeline with the LOIs, a capex and TI budget, and current sponsor financials. We're also ordering a new appraisal.
Nothing substantive until the PNL is signed. The servicer is gathering facts to run the NPV. It won't react to the ask yet.

Round 2 · After the appraisal ($62M as-is)

ServicerThe appraisal is $62 million against an $85M balance. A straight extension asks the trust to carry 100% of the risk on a loan that's 137% of value, while the equity keeps the upside. We could consider an extension with a $15M paydown, a hard lockbox with all excess cash trapped for leasing and paydown, a new interest-rate structure, and a modification fee.
The opening position anchors high. The real message is "the equity is out of the money; if you want the option, pay for it." "Pay to play" is the core principle of every modification.
Borrower$15M of paydown into a building appraised at $62M isn't rational for us. We'd be putting good money after bad. We can commit new capital, but it has to go into leasing, because that's what creates value for both of us. If the answer is $15M, we'll hand you the keys. Then you own a 64%-leased office building in a judicial foreclosure state with an 18-month timeline and no one to finish the lease-up.
The keys threat is the borrower's main leverage: foreclosure is slow and costly, and the servicer would have to hire a receiver, lease the building with a cold start, and sell into a weak office market. But it only works if the borrower's carve-out guaranty exposure is small.
ServicerWe'd prefer not to go that way either, but we're prepared to. Our analysis shows a deed-in-lieu or foreclosure recovers more than a straight extension. If we take the keys, we'll want a clean handover: cooperation agreement, estoppels, and confirmation there are no carve-out issues. Let's talk about what new capital actually looks like and how it would rank.
Calm counter-leverage: the servicer signals it's not afraid of foreclosure and quietly reminds the borrower about guaranty exposure. Then it opens the door to a structure, the "how it would rank" question.

Round 3 · Structuring

BorrowerHere's our proposal. We put in $14M: $6M paydown now and $8M into a leasing reserve. Split the loan into an A-note sized to today's value and a B-note for the rest. Extend three years. Our new money gets paid back with a return after the A-note but ahead of the B-note.
The classic A/B "hope note" modification. The sponsor will only put in new money if that money ranks ahead of old debt that's out of the money. Otherwise it's donating to the lender.
ServicerWe can work with that frame. Terms: $6M paydown and $8M leasing reserve at closing. A-note $55M, current pay at a market rate. B-note $24M, accruing, no current pay. Your new money earns an 8% pref after the A-note and ahead of the B-note, then everything goes to the B-note until repaid, then the residual splits. A three-year extension, with the last year conditioned on 80% leased. Hard lockbox, all excess cash to leasing costs then A-note paydown. You pay the modification fee and our legal. A sale or refinance needs our consent until the B-note is paid. And the guarantor reaffirms the carve-outs.
The servicer accepts the structure but tightens every lever: cash control, a performance hurdle for the final year, cost recovery, and a reaffirmed guaranty. Now it presents this to the controlling class with its NPV analysis.
BorrowerAgreed in principle, if the third-year test is 75% and leasing commissions are approved within ten business days.
The last round is about execution details. Approval speed matters a lot to a borrower trying to sign tenants.
The patternEach round moves from positions (extend vs. pay down) to interests (the borrower wants an option on recovery; the trust wants a higher NPV than foreclosure) to structure (new money that ranks ahead of the impaired old debt). Credible alternatives on both sides, keys vs. foreclosure, are what make the deal close.

Module 05

The options menu: everything short of (and including) foreclosure

Ordered roughly from least to most disruptive. Every option is a different split of the loss between the borrower, the lender and anyone else in the stack.

1 · Forbearance agreementTime-limited standstill

The lender agrees not to enforce for a set period (3–12 months) while the borrower sells, refinances or leases up. In return, the borrower usually pays something, accepts cash management and acknowledges the default. Fits: a short, specific gap, such as a sale under contract. Risk: it just delays the problem.

2 · Extension ("amend and extend")More time, at a price

Maturity is pushed out 1–3 years, usually with a paydown, an extension fee, a new rate cap, cash sweep and tighter covenants. Fits: a temporary market problem with an asset that's still near or above the loan amount. Criticism: "extend and pretend," when the value gap never closes.

3 · Rate or payment modificationLower debt service

The interest rate is cut, payments become interest-only, or some interest is deferred or capitalized (PIK). Fits: the property has value but can't cover current debt service. Cost: the lender gives up yield; bondholders at the bottom of a CMBS trust may lose interest.

4 · A/B note split ("hope note")Recognize the loss without forgiving it

The loan is split into an A-note sized to current value (current pay) and a B-note for the rest (accruing, paid only if value recovers). The borrower adds new money that ranks between them. Fits: a real value gap with an engaged sponsor and a credible recovery story. This is the most common large CMBS modification.

5 · Cash-in refinance / partial paydownSponsor writes a check

The borrower brings fresh equity to pay down the loan to a size a new lender will refinance. Fits: a sponsor with liquidity who still believes in the asset. It's the cleanest outcome for the lender: par recovery.

6 · Rescue capital / recapitalizationNew money from a third party

A rescue lender or investor provides pref equity or mezz to fill the gap, often with control rights. The senior lender must consent. Fits: a good asset, a sponsor short of cash. Cost: the original equity is diluted or wiped out.

7 · Discounted payoff (DPO)Take less now, done

The lender accepts less than the balance as full repayment, funded by a new lender or new equity, and releases the borrower. Fits: when the payoff beats the NPV of every other option, and the lender wants certainty. Tax note: forgiven debt can be taxable income to the borrower.

8 · Sale and assumptionNew sponsor, same (modified) loan

The property is sold to a new owner who assumes the loan, often modified and with new equity. Fits: the original sponsor is tired or broke, but a buyer sees value. The lender approves the new sponsor.

9 · Note saleThe lender exits; a buyer takes the problem

The lender sells the loan, often at a discount to the balance, to a distressed debt investor who then negotiates or forecloses ("loan-to-own"). Fits: a bank that wants the loan off its books, or a servicer that sees a sale price above its NPV of a workout. See Module 08.

10 · Deed-in-lieu of foreclosureKeys back, by agreement

The borrower deeds the property to the lender (or its designee) in exchange for a release from some or all liability. Fits: no equity left, a cooperative borrower. It's faster and cheaper than foreclosure, but the lender takes title subject to any junior liens. It often comes with a cooperation agreement and a "cash for keys" payment.

11 · Receivership + foreclosureEnforcement

A court-appointed receiver takes over management and rents while the lender forecloses. Non-judicial states (TX, CA, GA, AZ): roughly 2–6 months. Judicial states (NY, NJ, FL, IL): roughly 12–36 months. After foreclosure the property is REO (real estate owned) and is sold. Fits: no deal is possible, or the borrower is uncooperative or acting in bad faith.

12 · Borrower bankruptcyThe borrower's nuclear option

A Chapter 11 filing triggers the automatic stay, which halts foreclosure. For single-asset real estate, the debtor must, within 90 days, file a plausible plan or start paying interest, and it may try to "cram down" the loan to current value. But an SPE's voluntary filing usually triggers full recourse under the carve-out guaranty, which is why it's rare.

Leverage mapWhat each side can threaten

Borrower's leverage

  • It runs the asset and has the tenant relationships
  • Can hand back the keys (if guaranty exposure is small)
  • Can make foreclosure slow and expensive, especially in judicial states
  • Can offer new money, which the lender can't force it to contribute
  • Bankruptcy threat (blunted by carve-out guaranties)

Lender's leverage

  • Cash management: traps all excess cash
  • Default interest and fees keep accruing
  • Receiver: takes management and rents away from the borrower
  • Carve-out and other guaranties against the principal personally
  • Foreclosure wipes out the equity and any future upside
  • Reputation: lenders remember how sponsors behaved

Module 06

Choosing: the NPV test

The special servicer compares the present value of each path, using the Parkway numbers: an $85M loan, $62M appraisal. Change the assumptions and see which option wins.

Foreclose vs. DPO vs. A/B modification

How to read itWhat drives the answer

  • Foreclosure loses value through time (an 18-month judicial process), carry, legal and receiver costs, and a stigma discount on REO sales.
  • A DPO is certain and immediate, but locks in the loss. It wins when the offer is close to what foreclosure would net, or when the future is very uncertain.
  • A modification wins when the sponsor's new money and leasing effort raise the odds of recovery enough to beat both. Its value is very sensitive to the success probability, which is why servicers demand new money: it raises the probability and pays down the loan.
  • Different holders see different NPVs. The B-piece (most junior bonds) favors options that might recover more over time, while senior bondholders favor certainty. That tension is built into CMBS servicing.

Module 07 · Case studies

Case 1: Parkway Corporate Center (office, maturity default)

A 410,000 SF suburban office campus in New Jersey (a judicial foreclosure state). The $85M 10-year fixed CMBS loan from 2016 (4.30%, interest-only) matures in July 2026. The largest tenant (32% of space) left when its lease expired in 2025. Occupancy fell from 91% to 64%, and NOI from $7.4M to $4.6M. The loan still covers interest (DSCR ~1.26x) but can't be refinanced: a 5.4% debt yield is far below what any lender will accept.

TimelineWhat happened

WhenEvent
Jan 2026Borrower requests an extension. The master servicer transfers the loan to special servicing for imminent maturity default.
FebPNL signed. Information request. Hard lockbox triggered and excess cash trapped.
MarAppraisal: $62M as-is. ARA ≈ $85M − 90% × $62M ≈ $29M, which cuts interest advances on the most junior bonds.
Apr–MayNegotiation (Module 04). The servicer's NPV analysis: A/B modification ≈ $61M > DPO $57M > foreclosure ≈ $53M.
JunControlling class consulted; modification approved.
JulModification closes at the original maturity date.

OutcomeThe modified structure

1 · A-note $55MCurrent pay at ~6.0%, 3-year extension (third year needs 75% leased)
2 · Sponsor new money $14M + 8% pref$6M paydown + $8M leasing reserve
3 · B-note $24M (hope note)Accrues; paid only from sale or refi proceeds
4 · ResidualSplit between the lender and the sponsor

Balance after paydown: $85M − $6M = $79M = $55M A-note + $24M B-note. Every lever is tightened: hard lockbox, leasing approvals, a reaffirmed carve-out guaranty, and modification fees and legal costs paid by the borrower.

Who wins if it works?If the building leases to 85% and sells for $90M in 2029: A-note $55M is repaid. The sponsor gets back $14M plus ~$3.6M of pref. That leaves ~$17M for the B-note ($24M plus accrued interest), so a partial recovery on the hope note. Without the sponsor's $14M, the trust would likely have owned a 64%-leased REO building selling in the low $50s.
