Resolution: A/B modification with $14M of new sponsor money.

Case 2: Floating-rate apartment bridge loan

A $48M bridge loan (SOFR + 3.25%) on a 320-unit value-add apartment property, made in 2021 when SOFR was near zero. The Debt service rose from ~$1.6M a year at closing to ~$2.8M while its 2.5% SOFR cap held. Now the cap expires, replacing it costs $1.4M, and at ~4.3% SOFR debt service is ~$3.6M, while NOI is $3.1M because renovations lagged. DSCR falls to 0.86x. The balance-sheet lender (a debt fund) moves the loan to its asset-management workout team.

Option consideredOutcome
ForecloseValue ~$52M in a liquid multifamily market; a non-judicial state (TX) allows it in ~3 months. A recovery near par is possible, but the lender would become an owner-operator.
Sponsor cash-inSponsor can't fund it: equity committed elsewhere.
Rescue pref + modification (chosen)A third-party pref investor puts in $7M (13% accruing, control rights if the plan slips). $3M buys a 2-year rate cap and funds a debt-service reserve, $4M finishes renovations. The lender extends 18 months, cuts the spread 0.50% for a year, and takes a cash sweep. The original sponsor's equity is diluted but stays in.

Why it worked: the lender's basis (~$150k/unit) is well below replacement cost, so new capital is safe enough for a pref investor. The problem was cash flow and time, not value. This was a common pattern in 2023–25.

Module 08

Buying distressed debt

Banks and servicers sell troubled loans, singly or in pools, to investors who price them on expected resolution value, not on the balance. The buyer steps into the lender's rights: it can negotiate, foreclose, or sometimes recover more than it paid by pursuing guaranties.

What would you bid for the note?

Price = present value of what you expect to collect, at your target return.

Bid price
—
Cents on the dollar
—
Basis vs. resolution
—
Profit if as expected
—
Read
The seller sees the $85M balance; the buyer sees ~$60M of collateral, ~1.7 years, and costs. Your edge comes from knowing the asset better, moving faster than a regulated bank, or having a better plan for the property than the current owner. "Loan-to-own" buyers bid assuming they'll end up owning the asset at their basis.

DiligenceWhat a note buyer checks

  • Loan file: are the note, mortgage, assignments and guaranties complete and enforceable? Gaps in the chain of assignments slow foreclosure.
  • Collateral: fresh valuation, physical condition, leasing, and what it would take to stabilize.
  • Borrower and guarantor: cooperative or litigious? Is the guaranty collectable?
  • Jurisdiction: judicial vs. non-judicial foreclosure, receivership law, bankruptcy history.
  • Structure: mezz lenders with cure or purchase rights, intercreditor terms, tax liens or mechanic's liens ahead of you.

Module 09

Workout terminology

Special servicing transfer

Moving a CMBS loan from the master servicer to the special servicer when a trigger occurs.

Pre-negotiation letter (PNL)

Signed before talks: non-binding discussions, no waiver of defaults, only written agreements count.

Reservation of rights

Letter stating that accepting payments or talking doesn't waive the lender's remedies.

Appraisal Reduction Amount (ARA)

Roughly the loan balance minus 90% of the new appraised value. It reduces interest advances to the lowest CMBS classes.

Hope note / B-note

The part of a split loan above current value, paid only if the asset recovers.

Pay to play

A borrower must contribute new money to get concessions such as time, a rate cut or a loan split.

Extend and pretend

Extensions that delay a loss without a real plan to close the value gap.

Cash for keys

A payment to a borrower for a cooperative deed-in-lieu and handover.

Receiver

A court-appointed neutral party who manages the property and collects rents during enforcement.

REO

Real estate owned: property the lender (or trust) holds after foreclosure or deed-in-lieu.

Non-accrual

A bank loan on which interest is no longer recognized as income, usually at 90+ days delinquent.

Loan-to-own

Buying a loan with the goal of foreclosing and owning the property at the purchase basis.

Module 10

Self-check

Q1A borrower says, "We'll give you the keys tomorrow." When is that a strong threat, and when is it weak?

Reveal

Strong: judicial foreclosure state, a hard-to-operate asset (a half-leased office), little or no guaranty exposure, a weak market for REO sales. Weak: a non-judicial state, a liquid asset class (multifamily), a solvent guarantor with carve-out exposure, or a lender comfortable owning and operating.

Q2Why would a sponsor put $14M of new money into a building worth $23M less than its loan?

Reveal

Only if the new money ranks ahead of the impaired old debt (the B-note), earns a pref, and the sponsor believes leasing will raise value. It's buying a call option on recovery with senior protection. Also: avoiding a foreclosure on its record, keeping management fees, and protecting the guarantor.

Q3The DPO offer is $57M. The servicer's foreclosure NPV is ~$53M and the modification NPV is ~$61M with a 60% success chance. What happens if the success chance is really 30%?

Reveal

Run it in Module 06: at 30% the modification NPV falls to roughly $57.5M, about equal to the DPO. With equal NPVs, certainty usually wins, so the servicer would push for the DPO or ask for more new money to raise the odds.

Q4What's the first document signed in a CMBS workout, and why does it matter?

Reveal

The pre-negotiation letter. It stops either side claiming later that a conversation created a binding agreement or waived a default, so both can speak freely.

Q5You're a B-piece buyer and the controlling class. The special servicer recommends a DPO; you'd rather extend. Why might your view differ from the senior bondholders'?

Reveal

A DPO locks in a loss that falls first on your bonds, while seniors get paid in full either way. Extending keeps your position's option value alive. That conflict is why the servicing standard is "trust as a collective whole" and why an operating advisor reviews decisions.

Core concept · After-tax returns

Real Estate Tax

Real estate investors don't just earn returns; they keep them. Depreciation shelters income, 1031s defer gains, and property and transfer taxes can move value by millions. This tab covers US federal rules plus the three markets you're focused on: New York, New Jersey and Texas.

Taxes across the life of a deal

Buy: transfer taxes, mortgage recording tax

Hold: property tax, income tax sheltered by depreciation

Sell: capital gains, depreciation recapture, transfer taxes, or defer with a 1031

Educational summary as of Oct 2026. Rules change and every deal is fact-specific; confirm with a tax advisor or counsel.

Module 01

The tax map

Three layers of government tax real estate differently. Federal taxes the investor's income and gains. States add income tax (none in Texas) and transfer taxes. Local governments tax the property itself every year, and that's often the single biggest operating expense.

StageTaxWho sets itTypical size
AcquisitionTransfer / deed taxesState & city0% (TX) to ~3–4% (NYC commercial)
Mortgage recording taxNY state & cityUp to 2.8% of the loan (NYC commercial)
HoldProperty taxLocal (assessor, school district)~1–2.5% of value a year; 20–40% of operating expenses
Income tax on cash flowFederal + stateOften near zero early on, thanks to depreciation
SaleCapital gains + recapture + NIITFederal + stateUp to 20% / 25% / 3.8% federal, plus state
Transfer taxes (seller side)State & citySee Modules 07–10
Why a lender caresTaxes hit underwriting directly. A reassessment after a sale can raise property tax and cut NOI. An expiring abatement (421-a, PILOT, Ch. 312) is a scheduled NOI drop. Transfer and recording taxes are part of the sponsor's cost basis. Tax-driven deal timing (1031 deadlines) shapes how buyers behave.

Module 02

Depreciation & cost segregation

Buildings wear out, so the tax code lets owners deduct their cost over time, even while the property gains value. That non-cash deduction shelters cash flow from tax. Land never depreciates.

Residential rental

27.5 years, straight line, mid-month convention.

Nonresidential

39 years, straight line (office, retail, industrial, hotel).

Land improvements

15 years: parking lots, landscaping, site utilities.

Personal property

5 or 7 years: carpets, appliances, certain electrical and fixtures.

Cost segregationFaster deductions, legally

An engineering-based study reclassifies parts of the building from 27.5/39-year property into 5-, 7- and 15-year property, typically 15–35% of the building's cost. Since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 2025), 100% bonus depreciation is permanent for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, so those short-life components can be deducted entirely in year one. Bonus also applies to qualified improvement property (interior non-structural work on nonresidential buildings, 15-year).

Year-one deduction

Simplified: full-year convention, no state tax. It shows the order of magnitude.

Depreciable basis
—
No cost seg: yr-1 deduction
—
With cost seg + bonus
—
Extra tax deferred yr 1
—
Catch
It's a deferral, not a permanent saving. Every dollar deducted lowers your basis and comes back at sale as recapture (Module 03), unless you 1031 or hold until death. Deductions also only help if you can use them (passive loss rules, Module 05).

Other levers: §179 expensing for some property; repairs vs. capital improvements (repairs deductible now; improvements capitalized; safe harbors under the tangible property regulations); §179D energy-efficient building deduction and §45L new energy-efficient home credit, both ending for construction or acquisitions after June 30, 2026 under the 2025 law.

Module 03

Selling: capital gains & recapture

Gain = net sale price − adjusted basis (cost + improvements − depreciation taken). That gain is taxed in layers at different rates.

LayerWhat it isMax federal rate
§1245 recaptureDepreciation on personal property and cost-seg components, taxed as ordinary income37%
Unrecaptured §1250 gainStraight-line depreciation on the building25%
Long-term capital gainAppreciation above original cost (held more than a year)20%
Net investment income taxOn top, for higher earners not qualifying as active+3.8%
StateNY up to 10.9% (+3.876% NYC resident), NJ up to 10.75%, TX 0%varies

Tax on sale

Federal only. Shows why "depreciation now, recapture later" matters.

If the investor dies holding the property, heirs get a step-up in basis to fair market value (§1014): the deferred gain and recapture disappear. Hence the strategy "depreciate, 1031, repeat, die." An installment sale spreads gain over the years payments are received, but recapture is taxed in the year of sale.

Module 04

Deferral tools: 1031, 721, Opportunity Zones

§1031Like-kind exchange

Sell investment real estate and buy other investment real estate, and the gain (including recapture) is deferred, not forgiven. Since 2018 it applies only to real property. Any real estate held for investment or business use qualifies against any other: land for an apartment, an office for a warehouse.

  • Qualified intermediary (QI) holds the sale proceeds. If the seller touches the cash, the exchange fails.
  • 45 days to identify replacement property in writing: up to 3 properties of any value, or more under the 200% / 95% rules.
  • 180 days to close (or the tax return due date, if earlier, unless extended).
  • To defer fully, buy equal or greater value and replace the debt (or add cash). Cash or debt relief left over is boot, and it's taxable.
  • Same taxpayer on both sides; partnerships can't easily split partners into separate exchanges ("drop and swap" carries risk).
  • Variants: reverse exchange (buy first through an exchange accommodation titleholder), improvement exchange, DSTs (Delaware statutory trusts, fractional passive interests that qualify as replacement property).

1031 deadlines

Enter the closing date of the property you sold (the relinquished property).

Identification deadline (day 45)
—
Closing deadline (day 180)
—
Note
Deadlines are calendar days, with no extension for weekends or holidays (only federally declared disasters). If day 180 falls after your tax return due date, file an extension or the exchange period is cut short.

§721 UPREITContribute instead of sell

An owner contributes property to a REIT's operating partnership in exchange for OP units, tax-deferred under §721. OP units pay REIT-like distributions and can later be converted to REIT shares, which triggers the tax. It's popular for estate planning: hold OP units until death and get a step-up. A DST interest can later be rolled into an UPREIT (a "721 exchange").

Opportunity ZonesMade permanent in 2025

Original program (gains invested 2018–2026)OZ 2.0 (from Jan 1, 2027)
Designations~8,700 tracts, designated 2018Rolling 10-year designations, with tighter low-income tests
DeferralUntil Dec 31, 2026Rolling: 5 years after investment (or earlier sale)
Basis step-up10% / 15% (largely expired)10% after 5 years; 30% for rural funds
ExclusionHold the fund investment 10+ years and appreciation on it is tax-free (OZ 2.0 caps the benefit at 30 years)
Real estate ruleMust "substantially improve" existing buildings: invest more than the building basis within 30 months (50% for rural OZs under 2.0). Land doesn't count.

Mechanics: invest capital gains (not regular cash) within 180 days into a Qualified Opportunity Fund (QOF), which holds at least 90% of its assets in OZ property. Original-program deferred gains are recognized at the end of 2026, a known tax bill for many investors in early 2027.

Module 05

Entities & investor-level rules

LLC / partnership

The standard deal vehicle. Pass-through: one level of tax, losses flow to partners, flexible waterfalls (Capital Stack tab). Partners report income on a K-1.

REIT

No entity-level tax if it distributes 90% of taxable income and meets the 75% real-estate income and asset tests. Taxable REIT subsidiaries may hold up to 25% of assets from 2026.

C corporation

21% entity tax plus tax on dividends. Rare for holding real estate (double tax, no step-up for shareholders on assets).

§199A deduction

20% deduction on qualified business income and REIT dividends, made permanent in 2025. It cuts the top rate on REIT dividends to ~29.6%.

RuleWhat it doesWhy it matters
Passive activity rules (§469)Rental losses are passive and offset only passive income (with a $25k allowance phasing out for small "active" landlords)Depreciation losses can be trapped and carried forward until sale
Real estate professional status750+ hours and more than half of working time in real property trades, plus material participationLosses become non-passive and can offset W-2 or business income. Common for full-time developers and brokers.
§163(j) interest limitBusiness interest deductible up to 30% of EBITDA (restored and made permanent in 2025)Real estate can elect out (as a real property trade or business) but must then use longer ADS depreciation (30/40 yrs) and lose bonus on those assets
Carried interest (§1061)The sponsor's promote gets long-term rates only if held 3+ yearsPushes sponsors toward longer holds; unchanged in 2025
Debt-financed distributionsRefinance proceeds aren't taxable (it's a loan)Cash out tax-free while deferring gain: "buy, borrow, die"
FIRPTAForeign sellers: the buyer withholds 15% of the gross priceImportant in NYC and Miami deals; affects closing cash
LIHTC (2025 changes)State allocations +12%; the bond financing test drops from 50% to 25% from 2026More affordable deals pencil (Affordable Housing tab)

Module 06

Property tax: how it works, and what it does to value

Tax bill = assessed value × tax rate. Assessors estimate value (often by the income approach for commercial property), apply any assessment ratio or caps, and taxing bodies (city, county, school district, special districts) set rates to fund their budgets.

Assessment

Annual or periodic. Some places reassess on sale; some phase changes in; some have caps.

Exemptions & abatements

Reduce the taxable value or the bill for a period: affordable housing, new construction, economic development.

Appeals

Owners challenge value with income and comparable-sales evidence. Commercial owners appeal routinely, usually through tax certiorari attorneys on contingency.

Pass-through

In NNN leases, tenants reimburse taxes. In gross leases, the owner eats increases above the base year.

What a tax change does to value

Any permanent change in tax expense hits NOI dollar for dollar (unless passed through), and value by NOI ÷ cap rate. Abatements are temporary, so value their present value.

Value impact if permanent
—
Value impact if temporary
—
Read
A $150k/yr tax saving at a 5.5% cap is worth ~$2.7M if permanent. An abatement that lasts 15 years is worth less (its PV), and it ends with a cliff: when the abatement burns off, NOI drops. Lenders size loans on the unabated or post-burn-off tax at maturity.

ProgramForKey terms
485-x "Affordable Neighborhoods for New Yorkers" (2024; replaced 421-a)New rentals and conversions with 6+ units Very large (150+ units, Manhattan-heavy Zones A/B): 40-yr benefit, 25% affordable averaging 60% AMI, minimum construction wages ($72.45/hr Zone A, $63 Zone B, or a share of prevailing).
Large (100+): 35 yrs, 25% at avg 80% AMI, $40/hr minimum wage.
Modest (6–99): 35 yrs, 20% at avg 80% AMI.
Small (6–10, outside Manhattan): 10 yrs, half of units rent-stabilized.
Affordable units are permanent. Start construction by June 15, 2034; finish by June 15, 2038.
421-a(16) extensionProjects that started under the old programCompletion deadline extended to June 15, 2031 for vested projects
467-m (2024)Office-to-residential conversionsUp to ~35-yr exemption with 25% affordable at avg 80% AMI. Pairs with City of Yes conversion rules.
UAP (City of Yes, 2024)Zoning bonus~20% more floor area if the extra is permanently affordable (≤ 60% AMI average). Stacks with 485-x.
ICAPCommercial and industrial renovation or new construction outside core ManhattanAbates the increase in assessed value for up to 15–25 years
J-51 (revived 2022)Rental and co-op/condo capital improvementsExemption and abatement tied to affordability and rent regulation
Underwriting tip485-x's wage requirements and permanent affordability reduce NOI. The tax savings have to outweigh them. Model the abated tax schedule year by year, the wage premium in hard costs, and the restricted rents. Lenders will.

Module 08 · New Jersey

New Jersey

Transfer taxesThe 2025 "mansion tax" overhaul

New Jersey charges a realty transfer fee (RTF, graduated, paid by the seller, roughly 0.4–1.2% of price) plus a supplemental fee, the "mansion tax," on transfers over $1M of residential property and Class 4A commercial property (office, retail, industrial; apartment buildings in Class 4C are excluded). Since July 1, 2025, the mansion tax is graduated and paid by the seller (previously a flat 1% paid by the buyer):

PriceRate on full price
$1M – $2M1.0%
$2M – $2.5M2.0%
$2.5M – $3M2.5%
$3M – $3.5M3.0%
Over $3.5M3.5%

The same increase and shift to sellers applies to the controlling-interest transfer tax (selling 50%+ of an entity that owns NJ commercial property worth $1M+). On a $20M commercial sale, the seller now owes ~3.5% (~$700k) in supplemental fees alone, which changes pricing negotiations. NJ has no mortgage recording tax beyond nominal fees.

Property taxThe highest effective rates in the US

  • Average effective rate is about 2.2% of value. Assessments are at a municipal ratio to market (the equalization ratio), and many towns reassess or revalue periodically.
  • Chapter 91: the assessor can request income and expense data from income-producing property owners. Fail to respond within 45 days and you lose the right to appeal that year.
  • Appeals: file by April 1 (May 1 in towns with a revaluation). County tax board, or directly to Tax Court if the assessment exceeds $1M. Chapter 123 tests whether the assessment falls within ±15% of the equalized value.
  • Bulk sale notice: sellers of commercial property (and some residential) file form C-9600 with the Division of Taxation at least 10 business days before closing, or the buyer can become liable for the seller's state taxes.

PILOTsPayment in lieu of taxes: NJ's main development incentive

Long-Term Tax Exemption Law (N.J.S.A. 40A:20)

For projects in a designated redevelopment area (Entitlements tab, Module 05), built by an urban renewal entity. Instead of conventional tax, the owner pays an annual service charge, typically 10–15% of annual gross revenue (or ~2% of total project cost), for up to 30 years from completion, often stepping up toward full taxes in later stages. Profits are capped (typically 12%), with excess shared with the town. About 5% of the service charge goes to the county.

Five-Year Exemption & Abatement Law (40A:21)

Shorter abatements for improvements and new construction in areas in need of rehabilitation, phasing taxes in over about 5 years.

Why PILOTs are controversial, and why underwriters love themPILOT revenue mostly goes to the municipality, not school districts, so schools see little of it. For the owner, the service charge is predictable and often well below conventional tax: Jersey City, Newark and Harrison waterfront towers were largely built on PILOTs. Underwrite the PILOT schedule exactly, including the step-ups and the expiry.

State income tax: up to 10.75%. Non-resident sellers of NJ property pay estimated tax at closing (GIT/REP forms). Mount Laurel affordable-housing obligations shape where density is allowed (Entitlements tab).

Module 09 · Texas

Texas

Texas has no personal income tax, no transfer tax and no mortgage recording tax. The bill comes through property tax, which is high and is the main way local governments and schools are funded.

Effective rate

Often ~1.6–2.5% of value combined (city, county, school district, hospital, community college, MUD or special districts).

Non-disclosure state

Sale prices aren't public record. Appraisal districts estimate values from limited data, and owners can't easily be contradicted, which affects both protests and comps.

Franchise (margin) tax

Entity-level tax on revenue-based margin: 0.75% (0.375% retail/wholesale), with a no-tax-due threshold of ~$2.47M revenue. It hits LLCs and partnerships, not sole individuals.

Title insurance

Premiums are promulgated (set by the state). There's no price shopping on premium, only on service and endorsements.

The annual cycleAppraisal and protest

Jan 1Valuation date

Property valued as of January 1 by the county appraisal district (CAD).

Apr 15Renditions

Business personal property renditions due (extendable to May 15).

Apr–MayNotices of value

CAD mails appraised values.

May 15Protest deadline

Or 30 days after the notice. Informal meeting, then an Appraisal Review Board (ARB) hearing.

After ARBEscalate

Binding arbitration (for properties ≤ ~$5M), SOAH, or district court.

Oct–Jan 31Bills

Rates adopted in the fall; taxes due by January 31.

Commercial owners protest almost every year. Tax consultants work on contingency (often 25–35% of the savings).

Recent changes2023 and 2025 legislation

  • Circuit breaker: taxable value increases on non-homestead real property worth ≤ $5.32M (2026) are capped at 20% a year. It's a pilot program expiring December 31, 2026 and wasn't renewed in 2025. Underwrite a step-up risk for 2027.
  • Business personal property: the exemption rises from $2,500 to $125,000 from 2026 (Prop 9, approved November 2025). No rendition is needed below that.
  • Homestead exemption for school taxes: $140,000 (from 2025). School M&O tax rates were compressed with state funds.
  • 2025 procedural changes: automatic refunds, 12% interest on late refunds, video ARB hearings, and binding arbitration for tenants contractually responsible for taxes.

IncentivesHow Texas competes for projects

ToolWhat it does
Ch. 312 tax abatementCities and counties abate up to 100% of the increase in value for up to 10 years in a reinvestment zone
Ch. 380 / 381 agreementsFlexible city/county economic development grants and loans, often rebating sales or property tax
TIRZ (tax increment reinvestment zone)Captures future tax growth in a district to fund its infrastructure
JETI (Ch. 403, 2023)Replaced the expired Ch. 313 school-tax limitations for large manufacturing and energy projects. Narrower: excludes renewables and most real estate.
MUDs (municipal utility districts)Fund suburban water, sewer and road infrastructure with bonds repaid by residents' property taxes, often adding 0.5–1.0% to the rate in new subdivisions
Freeport exemptionExempts inventory shipped out of state within 175 days. Important for logistics.
Affordable housing (PFC / HFC)Public facility corporations co-own projects, granting 100% property tax exemption in exchange for affordable units. Reformed in 2023 after scrutiny.

Also from 2025: SB 17 bars entities from designated countries (China, Iran, North Korea, Russia) from acquiring Texas real property. That's a diligence item for foreign buyers.

Module 10

Closing-tax calculator: NYC vs. NJ vs. Texas

The same purchase in three markets. Transfer and recording taxes are a real cost that buyers and sellers price in. They can reach about 5% of value on a leveraged NYC commercial deal and are zero in Texas.

Estimate transaction taxes

Rates as of late 2026: NYS 0.4% / 0.65%; NYC RPTT 1–2.625%; NYC mansion tax 1–3.9% (buyer); NYC mortgage recording tax 2.05–2.8%; NJ mansion and supplemental fee 1–3.5% (seller, from July 2025). NJ's base realty transfer fee is graduated, so it's shown as an estimate. Estimates only, excluding title insurance, recording fees, and local quirks. Confirm with the title company.

Module 11

Self-check

Q1An investor buys a $20M apartment building, does a cost seg study, and takes $4M of bonus depreciation in year one. Is that $4M saved forever?

Reveal

No. It's deferred. Basis drops by $4M, and on sale that portion is recaptured as ordinary income (§1245, up to 37%), not at the 25% or 20% rates. It becomes permanent only via a 1031 chain ending in a step-up at death, or if the investor's rate at sale is lower.

Q2A sponsor's NYC multifamily pro forma assumes the 485-x benefit. What should a lender underwrite?

Reveal

The year-by-year tax schedule including any phase-out, restricted rents on the affordable units (permanent), the wage premium in construction costs, and the risk the benefit isn't granted (eligibility, deadlines, compliance). Size the loan on NOI that's realistic at maturity, not only on peak abated NOI.

Q3Why might a Texas apartment owner worry about 2027 even with no change in the building?

Reveal

The 20% circuit breaker on non-homestead property ≤ $5.32M expires after 2026. Properties whose appraised value outran the cap could see a jump in taxable value, and taxes, in 2027 unless the legislature renews it.

Q4A seller is choosing between a $20M sale of a Newark office building in 2026 and an entity (controlling-interest) sale. How do NJ's 2025 changes affect the choice?

Reveal

Both now carry the graduated supplemental fee (3.5% above $3.5M) paid by the seller, because the controlling-interest tax was raised and shifted the same way. The old trick of selling the entity to avoid the buyer-paid fee no longer helps, and the seller should price ~$700k of supplemental fees into its net proceeds.

Core concept · Where value is created

Entitlements & Development

Entitlements are the government approvals that let you build a particular project on a particular site. Winning them is often the single biggest value jump in a development, and the riskiest. This tab covers the zoning toolkit, the approval process in New York City, New Jersey and Texas, and how developers, investors and lenders price entitlement risk.

The development sequence

Land → control the site (option or contract)

Entitle → zoning, environmental review, site plan

Permit & finance → building permits, construction loan

Build & stabilize → construction, lease-up, refinance or sell

Educational summary as of Oct 2026. Local rules change often; confirm with land-use counsel.

Module 01

Why entitlements matter

Land is worth what you're allowed to build on it. The same acre can be worth $1M as a parking lot and $15M with approvals for 300 apartments. A developer's core skill is buying land at its current-use value and selling (or building on) it at its entitled value.

Stage 1Raw land

Current zoning, unknown feasibility. Cheapest, highest risk.

Stage 2Entitled

Zoning and land-use approvals in hand. Biggest step up in value.

Stage 3Shovel-ready

Permits issued, utilities confirmed, site plan approved, financing lined up.

Stage 4Stabilized

Built and leased. Valued on NOI ÷ cap rate.

What "entitled" includes

Zoning (use, density, height), any variances or special permits, environmental clearance, site plan or subdivision approval, and agreements (redeveloper, PILOT, development agreement).

Who grants them

Local government mostly: planning boards, zoning boards, city councils. State and federal agencies for environmental, wetlands, coastal and historic issues.

Why it's risky

Discretion and politics. A community board, council member or neighborhood group can delay or kill a project. Timelines are uncertain and carrying costs pile up.

Vesting

The point at which rights are locked in against future rule changes. Varies by state: often at permit issuance or substantial construction (NY), at preliminary approval (NJ), or at first permit application (TX, Ch. 245).

The key distinctionAs-of-right: the project complies with existing zoning, so approval is ministerial (a building permit). Discretionary: it needs a variance, special permit or rezoning, which means public hearings, environmental review, votes, and risk. Every deal underwrites very differently depending on which one it is.

Module 02

The zoning toolkit

Zoning controls use (what), bulk (how much and what shape) and parking and design (how).

TermMeaningExample
FAR (floor area ratio)Zoning floor area ÷ lot area20,000 SF lot × FAR 6.0 = 120,000 SF buildable
Height & setbackMax height, street-wall rules, sky exposure planesCan limit how much of the FAR you can actually fit
Lot coverage / open spaceShare of the lot a building can coverPushes density up rather than out
Parking minimumsRequired spaces per unit or per SFEliminated in much of NYC (2024); capped in large Texas cities on converted commercial sites (2025)
Density bonusExtra FAR for providing affordable housing, plazas, transit improvementsNYC Universal Affordability Preference (~20% extra)
Transferable development rights (TDR) / air rightsUnused FAR sold from one lot to another (usually adjacent, or within a special district)Buying air rights from a church or landmark next door
Zoning lot mergerCombining adjacent tax lots into one zoning lot to share FARThe common NYC way to move air rights
Nonconforming use / bulkLegal before the current rules; "grandfathered" but can't expand, and may lose status if abandoned or destroyedUnderwriting risk if a building can't be rebuilt as-is after a casualty

ReliefWhen the project doesn't fit

Variance

Permission to deviate from the rules because of a hardship unique to the property (an odd lot shape, topography). Granted by a board of appeals (NYC BSA, NJ zoning board). Use variances (allowing a use the zone prohibits) are much harder than bulk (area) variances (setbacks, height, coverage).

Special permit / conditional use

A use the zone allows only if specified conditions are met. Reviewed case by case, usually with a hearing.

Rezoning (map amendment)

Change the zoning district itself. A legislative act by the city council: the most discretionary and political route, but also the biggest value creator.

PUD / development agreement

A negotiated, project-specific package: site plan, density and public benefits bundled together. Common in Texas and suburban NJ for master-planned projects.

Module 03

Residual land value: pricing what you can build

Developers value land backward: what the finished project is worth, minus what it costs to build, minus the profit needed to take the risk. What's left is the most you can pay for the land. Change the FAR and you change the land value. That's entitlement value.

Residual land value

As-of-right vs. upzoned. Rental project valued at stabilization.

Reading itWith value and cost per SF held constant, every buildable SF is worth the same (about $86 here), which is why developers pay so much attention to price per buildable SF ("per FAR foot"), the standard way land is quoted in NYC and other dense markets. In reality the extra floors are worth less than the first ones: taller buildings cost more per SF (concrete frames, more elevators), and rezonings come with Mandatory Inclusionary Housing, so the true uplift is usually smaller than this simple calculator shows. If residual value is below what the seller wants, the project doesn't pencil: lower the price, add density, cut cost, or walk away.

Simplified: ignores financing cost during construction, lease-up and abatements. A full model is a development pro forma with a monthly construction draw schedule.

Module 04

Environmental & other approvals

ReviewApplies toWhat it involves
NEPA (federal)Projects with federal funding, permits or land (HUD financing, Army Corps permits)Categorical exclusion, environmental assessment, or full EIS
SEQRA (NY State)Discretionary actions by NY agenciesShort or full environmental assessment form; a "positive declaration" requires an EIS
CEQR (NYC)Discretionary NYC actions (rezonings, special permits)EAS, then EIS if significant impacts; the EIS can take 12–24 months and drives the ULURP schedule
NJ DEPWetlands, flood hazard areas, coastal zones (CAFRA, waterfront development)Permits; the state's climate-resilience (REAL) rules push design flood elevations higher in tidal areas, adding cost to waterfront projects
TexasNo state environmental review statuteFederal rules only (wetlands, endangered species); TCEQ permits for specific issues

Phase I ESA

Required by lenders and to qualify for CERCLA liability defenses. Identifies "recognized environmental conditions." A Phase II tests soil and groundwater.

Brownfields

NY Brownfield Cleanup Program (tax credits, liability release); NJ requires a Licensed Site Remediation Professional (LSRP) and issues Response Action Outcomes. Texas has a Voluntary Cleanup Program.

Historic / landmarks

NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission must approve work on landmarks and in historic districts. Section 106 review applies if federal money is involved.

Infrastructure

Utility capacity (sewer moratoria in parts of NJ), traffic studies, school impact. In Texas suburbs, MUD creation to fund water and sewer.

Module 05 · New York City

New York City

The NYC Zoning Resolution governs every lot. As-of-right projects go straight to the Department of Buildings (DOB) for permits. Anything discretionary goes through ULURP or the BSA.

ULURPUniform Land Use Review Procedure

Required for rezonings, special permits from the City Planning Commission, city property sales and leases, and major public facilities. The clock starts only when the Department of City Planning certifies the application complete. Pre-certification work (scoping, the CEQR EIS, negotiations) often takes 1–2 years.

Day 0Certification

DCP certifies the application and environmental review.

60 daysCommunity board

Hearing and advisory vote.

30 daysBorough president

Advisory recommendation.

60 daysCity Planning Commission

Hearing and binding vote: approve, modify, or deny.

50 daysCity Council

Reviews CPC approvals of rezonings (automatically) and others if it chooses. By tradition the council defers to the local member ("member deference"), which makes that one council member the key vote.

5 + 10 daysMayor

May veto; the council can override with two-thirds.

Total formal review: about 7 months. Rezonings that add housing trigger Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (MIH): 20–30% of units permanently affordable.

Recent reformsA more pro-housing system

  • City of Yes for Housing Opportunity (Dec 2024): the Universal Affordability Preference (about 20% more FAR for affordable units), elimination of parking requirements for new housing in much of the city, ADUs, "town center" and transit-oriented housing in lower-density areas, and easier office-to-residential conversions (buildings built before 1991). Projected to add roughly 80,000 homes over 15 years.
  • Charter revision, November 2025: voters approved a fast-track for publicly financed affordable housing in the community districts that produce the least of it (moving it out of ULURP to the BSA), an expedited land use review (ELURP) for modest housing and infrastructure projects that's about half as long and skips council review, and an Affordable Housing Appeals Board that can override council denials.
  • Neighborhood rezonings: Midtown South (2025), SoHo/NoHo (2021), Gowanus (2021) and others create large as-of-right capacity, so land values change overnight.

BSA

Board of Standards and Appeals: variances (five findings, including unique hardship and no reasonable return under current zoning) and certain special permits. Not part of ULURP.

Air rights

Zoning lot mergers and TDRs are a big market. Air rights trade at a large share of land value per buildable SF.

DOB

Plan approval and permits. "Zoning challenges" by neighbors can halt as-of-right projects. Vesting generally requires substantial construction.

Taxes tie-in

Most new rental feasibility depends on 485-x plus UAP. See the Real Estate Tax tab.

Module 06 · New Jersey

New Jersey

New Jersey has 560+ municipalities, each with its own zoning under the state Municipal Land Use Law (MLUL). "Home rule" means land use is intensely local, but two state frameworks dominate dense development: redevelopment and Mount Laurel.

MLULThe two boards

Planning board

Master plan, site plan and subdivision approvals, conditional uses, and "c" (bulk) variances tied to a site plan. Statutory deadlines: generally 45 days for minor and 95–120 days for preliminary major applications after completeness. Miss them and the application is deemed approved.

Zoning board of adjustment

Variances. A "d" (use) variance needs 5 of 7 votes and "special reasons" plus a showing of no substantial detriment to the public good or zone plan: the hardest approval to win. "c" variances need hardship or a better-planning rationale.

Preliminary site plan approval vests zoning for 3 years; final approval for 2 years (with extensions). Neighbors challenge approvals in court through an action in lieu of prerogative writs within 45 days of publication of the decision.

RedevelopmentThe Local Redevelopment and Housing Law

  1. Investigation: the governing body asks the planning board to study whether an area qualifies as an "area in need of redevelopment" (statutory criteria: deterioration, obsolete layout, underused land, etc.) or "in need of rehabilitation."
  2. Designation: council resolution, as a condemnation or non-condemnation area. Only condemnation areas allow eminent domain.
  3. Redevelopment plan: adopted by ordinance; it supersedes zoning and sets use, density and design. Often written around a specific project.
  4. Redeveloper agreement: a contract naming the designated redeveloper, with obligations, timelines and public benefits.
  5. Financial agreement (PILOT): a separate ordinance granting the long-term tax exemption (Real Estate Tax tab, Module 08).

This is how Jersey City, Newark, Harrison, Hoboken and New Brunswick built most of their towers: designation + plan + PILOT gives a developer zoning certainty and tax certainty.

Mount LaurelAffordable housing obligations

The NJ Supreme Court's Mount Laurel decisions require every town to provide its "fair share" of regional affordable housing. A 2024 law (P.L. 2024, c. 2) abolished COAH, set a formula-based process run by the Department of Community Affairs, and created a dispute-resolution program for the fourth round (July 2025 – June 2035). Towns adopt housing plans and rezone sites, usually as inclusionary zoning (typically 20% affordable for sale, 15% for rental). Towns that don't comply risk builder's remedy lawsuits, in which a court lets a developer build at high density.

Why it matters for dealsMount Laurel sites often come with as-of-right multifamily zoning at densities the town would never approve otherwise, which makes them some of the best suburban NJ multifamily opportunities.

Module 07 · Texas

Texas

Texas is the most permissive of the three, and since 2023–2025 the state legislature has repeatedly overridden cities to make building easier.

Houston: no zoning

No use zoning, but development is still regulated: deed restrictions (enforced by the city), the Chapter 42 subdivision ordinance (lot sizes, setbacks), parking rules and building codes. Small-lot townhomes are common.

Counties

Counties have no zoning power. Unincorporated suburban growth is shaped by platting rules, MUDs and deed restrictions.

Shot clock

Cities must approve or deny plats and site plans within 30 days (HB 3167, 2019), and since 2023 applicants can use third-party reviewers if a city misses deadlines (HB 3699).

Vested rights (Ch. 245)

A project is governed by the rules in effect when the first permit application is filed. Strong protection against rule changes mid-project.

2025 legislaturePro-housing laws (effective Sept 1, 2025)

BillWhat it does
SB 840In large cities (population over 150k in counties over 300k), allows multifamily and mixed-use by right on land zoned commercial, office, retail or warehouse, with at least 36 units/acre and 45-foot height allowed; converting commercial buildings to residential is allowed; parking limited to 1 space per unit
SB 15Large cities must allow small single-family lots (as small as 3,000 SF) in new subdivisions
HB 24Neighbor protests against rezonings that add housing need 60% of nearby landowners (was 20%), and council can approve by simple majority (was three-quarters)
SB 17Bars entities tied to designated foreign adversary countries from buying Texas real property

MUDsHow suburban Texas gets built

A developer creates a municipal utility district (by the TCEQ or the legislature), fronts the cost of water, sewer and drainage, and is reimbursed from tax-exempt bonds the MUD issues once homes are built and the tax base exists. Residents pay the MUD tax rate on top of city, county and school taxes. For a land developer, MUD reimbursements can return a large share of infrastructure spending, a major part of master-planned community economics around Houston, Dallas and Austin.

Annexation: since 2019 cities need consent to annex, and since 2023 (SB 2038) landowners can petition out of a city's extraterritorial jurisdiction (ETJ), escaping city development rules.

Module 08

Timelines: same project, three markets

Illustrative schedule for a ~300-unit rental project, from land control to stabilization. Hatched bars are the stages with the most schedule risk.

Why time is moneyEvery month of entitlement delay costs land carry (interest or opportunity cost), pursuit costs (lawyers, architects, consultants, studies) and market risk: rents, construction costs and interest rates can all move against you before you break ground.

Module 09

Land deals: who takes the entitlement risk?

StructureHow it worksRisk to the developer
Buy outrightPay full price at closing, then pursue approvalsHighest: owns the land if denied
Contract with entitlement contingencyClosing conditioned on obtaining approvals; extended due diligenceLow: walks if denied (loses deposit or pursuit costs). Sellers demand a higher price.
OptionPay a fee for the right to buy at a set price within a period; extension paymentsLimited to the option fee and pursuit costs
Land bankingA land banker buys and holds lots; the builder takes them down over timeOff balance sheet; common for homebuilders in Texas
Seller participation / JVLandowner contributes land for equity or a share of the upsideShared; aligns the seller with the approval
Ground leaseLease the land (often 99 years) instead of buyingLower upfront cost; needs a leasehold-financeable lease

The entitlement bet

Buy now vs. option-and-entitle. Expected value, ignoring discounting.

If denied, the buy-now developer still owns land worth roughly its as-is value (often less: a failed application can stigmatize a site). The option holder walks away, losing only the fee and pursuit costs. The seller charges for that protection through a higher strike price.

Module 10

The lender's view of entitlement risk

Most lenders won't finance entitlement risk with senior debt. Construction loans close only when the project is fully approved and permitted. Before that, capital is equity or expensive land loans.

StageTypical capitalLeverage
Pre-entitlement landSponsor equity, land funds, high-yield land loans (debt funds)0–50% LTV of as-is value; rates often 10%+
Entitled, pre-constructionPre-development loans, land loans; value now based on entitled landUp to ~50–65% of entitled land value
ConstructionBanks, debt funds; equity goes in first55–70% of cost; completion guaranty and carry guaranty
StabilizedAgency, CMBS, life company, bank refinance60–75% LTV, DSCR-based

Closing conditions

Final approvals, with appeal periods expired (NJ's 45-day window, an Article 78 window in NY); building permits issued; zoning report or zoning opinion letter.

Zoning diligence

A zoning report (PZR or similar) confirms the use is permitted, the building is compliant or legally nonconforming, and whether it could be rebuilt after a casualty.

Abatement diligence

485-x eligibility letters, the PILOT ordinance and financial agreement (and whether it survives foreclosure and transfers to the lender or a new owner).

Distress angle

Entitlements can lapse (expired approvals, missed 485-x deadlines). A special servicer or note buyer values a stalled site on what is still vested (Distressed Debt tab).

Module 11 · Illustrative case

"Harbor Street": a Jersey City redevelopment

A hypothetical, simplified case that ties zoning, tax and finance together. Numbers are illustrative.

The site: a 1.2-acre (52,000 SF) former warehouse near a PATH station, zoned light industrial. As-is value about $9M.

The plan: 380 rental units in a 28-story tower (~420,000 GSF, FAR ~8).

Months 0–3Contract with contingency

Developer signs a contract at $16M, conditioned on redevelopment approvals and a PILOT, with a $500k deposit that goes hard after 90 days.

Months 2–8Designation & plan

City council has the planning board investigate; the site is designated a non-condemnation redevelopment area. A redevelopment plan allowing residential at FAR 8 is adopted by ordinance.

Months 7–12Redeveloper & financial agreements

Redeveloper agreement: 10% affordable units (city inclusionary rule), a public plaza, local hiring. PILOT ordinance: service charge of 11% of gross revenue for years 1–10, stepping to 12–14% and then a phase-in toward full taxes through year 30.

Months 11–15Site plan & permits

Planning board site plan approval (no variances needed, because the plan sets the rules). The 45-day appeal window passes with no challenge.

Month 16Close land & construction loan

Land closes at $16M. Construction loan sized at ~60% of a ~$260M cost, with conventional-tax and PILOT scenarios both underwritten.

PILOT vs. conventional tax

Questions to think through: Why did the developer accept a hard deposit before approvals? (Competitive land, a supportive city.) What happens to value as the PILOT steps up? (Buyers value the declining abatement, not year-1 NOI.) How would a lender size the take-out loan in year 10?

Module 12

Self-check

Q1A seller in Brooklyn quotes land at $250 per buildable SF. What do you need to check before accepting "buildable"?

Reveal

Whether the FAR is actually usable as-of-right (height and setback limits, lot shape), whether it assumes bonuses (UAP requires permanently affordable units), any air rights already sold or available to buy, landmark or special district rules, and whether the deal relies on 485-x. Price per buildable SF only means something if the buildable area is real.

Q2Why do NJ developers prefer a redevelopment plan to a "d" variance?

Reveal

A redevelopment plan supersedes zoning by ordinance, so no variance is needed and the project needs only site plan approval. It's paired with a redeveloper agreement and usually a PILOT. A d variance needs 5 of 7 zoning board votes, special reasons proof, and is more exposed to appeal.

Q3A Texas developer wants to build 250 apartments on a strip-mall site in Dallas in 2026. What changed?

Reveal

Under SB 840 (2025), multifamily is allowed by right on commercially zoned land in large cities, at a density of at least 36 units/acre and 45 ft height, with parking capped at 1 space per unit. No rezoning is needed, which removes the main entitlement risk. HB 24 also makes it harder for neighbors to block rezonings that add housing.

Q4A construction lender is asked to close the day after a NJ planning board approval. What's the problem?

Reveal

The 45-day window for an action in lieu of prerogative writs hasn't run (it starts on publication of the resolution). A neighbor lawsuit could overturn the approval. Lenders typically require the appeal period to expire, or title and zoning protection, before funding.
